note: Portrait plate, upright in the scan. Seven groups: 1. 'Nos 1.2.3.4.5 & 6 - Rain Water Pipes, Abbot's Hospital, Guildford, Surrey.' Six LEAD cistern-heads (hopper heads) with their pipes, drawn in perspective-ish elevation with heavy hatching for the lead. No.1: a box head whose top is CRENELLATED (merlon-and-embrasure cresting) with two projecting side wings; the front face is a plain sunk panel; below, a tapering shoe/funnel gathers into the pipe; two flat fixing straps with nail holes stand out at the sides; the pipe below has a moulded band. No.3: box head with a stepped top and two side wings; the front face is a plain panel; below the head a HEART-SHAPED cartouche or trefoil ornament is cast on the shoe; the pipe passes through a moulded rectangular collar. No.4: head with a strongly panelled front (three vertical sunk slots) and a FAN or fluted apron below, gathering into a moulded rectangular collar and then the pipe; a second collar lower down marks a pipe joint. No.5: head with an embattled cresting of small merlons, then two horizontal reeded/roll bands, then an ogee-moulded lower body which sweeps out to a swan-neck offset, with a further collar where it meets the vertical pipe. subject: Notre-Dame de Paris, choir roof (not later than 1220): elevation of the hip ferme-maîtresse
note: fig. 9 | DRAWING: geometrical elevation, half-truss about a centre line | SEEN: Half of the hip truss. Poinçon G on the centre line; great arbalétrier E; SOUS-ARBALÉTRIER F set below and parallel to it; three entraits retroussés stacked up the truss (H lowest, then I, then K near the apex); the entrait L at the bottom SUSPENDED from the poinçon by moises M with wooden keys and by two pairs of vertical moises N; a further pair of moises O replacing the jambettes and clamping rafter to tie; liens P at the foot carrying part of the tie's weight onto posts set against the bahut. Note the second entrait retroussé I is drawn as a PAIR of pieces embracing the other members (a moise), whereas H and K are single tenoned members. Eyeball geometry: half-span ~285 px, rise ~480 px -> pitch about 59 deg. | FACTORY: Rich part list for a 'ferme de croupe': poinçon, arbalétrier, sous-arbalétrier, 3x collar at roughly equal intervals up the rafter, tie, 4 moise pairs, 2 foot liens onto posts. The design rule Viollet states is SPACING OF THE COLLARS: 'la flexion des arbalétriers est arrêtée à intervalles égaux par les trois entraits retroussés' - collars at EQUAL intervals is a buckling-length rule, not an aesthetic one. Also: the foot liens P must be placed directly over the external flying buttresses ('au droit des arcs-boutants') or they push the wall - a placement constraint that couples roof to buttress spacing. | VERIFICATION: pitch ~61 deg. The 'a intervalles egaux' sentence belongs to THIS truss only - full text 'La flexion des arbalETriers DE CETTE FERME est donc arretee a intervalles egaux par les trois entraits retrousses, rendus rigides eux-memes par les sous-arbaletriers.' The reader elided 'de cette ferme' and promoted it to a universal invariant. Equal collar spacing is an observation about this Notre-Dame hip truss, not a rule.

subject: Notre-Dame de Paris, choir roof: longitudinal section on the axis of the chevet, showing how the hip truss is held in its vertical plane
note: fig. 10 | DRAWING: longitudinal section (coupe) through the axis | SEEN: Masonry vault extrados S drawn at the bottom - this roof sits over stone vaults, no part of it is seen from inside. Q = the hip ferme-maîtresse of fig.9, standing at the left; R = the fan of hip rafters butting against its head from one side only. To hold Q upright the carpenters ran a long inclined piece T-U from the sablières up to a scarf at V, continued by V-X into the head of the poinçon of the FIFTH ferme-maîtresse back; from that point two pieces splayed as a V carry the thrust down onto the ends of a tie. T-U is itself hung from poinçon Q and from two faux poinçons Y, Z by heavy moises and keys, and three contrefiches C' are footed on it to prop the hip. Entrait D' with moise pair F' holds the curved hip sablières; entraits retroussés K', axial entretoises R', double entretoises P', liens H' against rolling. | FACTORY: This is the HIP RESTRAINT recipe and it reaches five bays back into the roof - a hip is not a local operation. Also record Viollet's verdict on it: 'un expédient', and that this frame has 'pas de solidarité entre les fermes' - with the boarding off you can move the trusses BY HAND. So for a 1220-date roof the correct structural model is: the volige (boarding) is the diaphragm; the timber bracing alone is inadequate.

subject: Westminster Hall: perspective of one whole bay between two fermes-maîtresses
note: fig. 33 | DRAWING: perspective construction view | SEEN: Looking up into one bay. The principal panne course O is set on the HEADS of the posts D, relieved by liens L and claire-voie infill; goussets M tie the collar A to that panne; the principal course is doubled by a projecting plateau on which jambettes are tenoned to stop the rafters above the dormers sliding. The other panne courses I are relieved by curved liens N lying in the plane of the rafters and tenoned into the arbalétriers. The lowest panne course I' is additionally propped by contrefiches P bearing on the EXTRADOS of the great curved moise, because that course carries the dormer roofs R as well as the rafters. Dormer R with traceried cheek visible at left; the stone wall, window and the wall arcading are drawn behind. | FACTORY: This is the figure that shows how a 5.75 m truss spacing is made to work: the pannes get liens in the roof plane, goussets to the collar, and contrefiches off the moise extrados. Rafter count is stated: ELEVEN chevrons between fermes -> 12 intervals over 5.75 m -> chevron spacing about 0.48 m, which is inside the French 0.45-0.63 band even though the trusses are ten times further apart.

subject: Westminster Hall, one ferme-maîtresse (the hammer-beam system at its fullest)
note: fig. 32 | DRAWING: geometrical half-elevation with 5 m scale bar | SEEN: Half truss about a dotted centre line, drawn with all its tracery. NO entrait. A single-piece entrait retroussé A (collar), thicker at mid-length than at its ends ('posé sur son fort'). The triangle above the collar is completely filled with claire-voie tracery and is a closed rigid unit. It stands on two posts D whose feet are tenoned onto the projecting end of the blochet (hammer-beam) E; E is held level by the great curved lien F which runs down to a carved corbel; the whole lower zone is clamped by IMMENSE CURVED MOISES H which embrace the middle of the collar A, the post D, the blochet E and the foot of the lien F, so the half-truss becomes one board. Pannes I on the way up. Every spandrel is filled with vertical tracery. Geometry from the stated numbers: span 21.00 in-oeuvre, 14.00 wall head to ridge -> pitch 53.1 deg, half-rafter 17.5 m against the stated 17.00 m including tenons. | FACTORY: The reference ENGLISH/ANGLO-NORMAN great-hall truss. Parametric core: half_span 10.50, rise_above_wallhead 14.00, pitch 53 deg, no tie. Its logic (Viollet's own statement of the problem, fig 30) is: give two rigid triangles A and B a COMMON BASE C-D, and you can dispense with a tie joining their apexes. Implementation = collar in one piece + tracery infill + curved clamping moises. The tracery is STRUCTURAL here, not decoration: 'les remplissages verticaux sont autant d'ordonnées qui, par leur pression verticale, empêchent les courbes de se déformer'. | VERIFICATION: atan(14.00/10.50) = 53.1 deg confirmed as ARITHMETIC on stated numbers, not a measurement. Eleven chevrons per bay confirmed in the text.

subject: Anglo-Norman truss without a tie, for a larger span: two curved braces assembled one above the other
note: fig. 29 | DRAWING: geometrical half-elevation with a written dimension 4,50 | SEEN: Half truss about a dotted centre line. Faux poinçon at the head with the collar tenoned into it; a heavy arbalétrier; and beneath it TWO curved pieces assembled one above the other (because a single courbe of that length could not be found), the upper one struck to a flatter radius; a horizontal member (panne or hammer-beam level piece) projecting inward; the whole footed on a moulded blochet on the wall head, drawn with the keyed sablières. Written dimension 4,50 from the centre line to the wall. Eyeball pitch about 53 deg. | FACTORY: Anglo-Norman kit: NO ENTRAIT, faux poinçon, arbalétrier + one or two courbes trapping the pannes between them, moulded blochet. Rule from the text: use ONE courbe up to about 5.40 m span; above that, two courbes stacked, with heavier scantlings so the tenons are strong enough. The 4,50 annotation implies a total span near 9 m for the two-courbe version. | VERIFICATION: pitch measures ~53 deg (English), i.e. the same as the Westminster arithmetic - but see Ely at 63 deg: the English range OVERLAPS the French one and pitch is not a region discriminator.

subject: Ely cathedral, nave and transepts, late 14th c: one ferme and the bay between fermes
note: fig. 31 | DRAWING: half elevation of a ferme (right) + the entre-deux des fermes (left), 5 m scale bar | SEEN: Right: half truss. One great courbe A-B in a SINGLE piece from the big blochet C up to the faux poinçon D. The triangular voids E, F between courbe and arbalétrier are filled with madriers (thick planks) rebated under the rafter and into the back of the curve, making curve and rafter act together. Pannes are trapped between rafter and courbe. Sous-faîte G with curved liens. The blochet is held level by a curved lien H bearing on a potelet I carved as a shaft and on a corbelet K built into the wall - so the thrust is taken BELOW the wall head. A timber cornice with a frieze of half-figures of angels holding shields masks the plates. Left: the panelled bay between trusses. | FACTORY: Encode the ANGEL CORNICE and the potelet/corbelet pair - both are strong English-Gothic silhouette cues. Structural rule Viollet states: strength here comes from the size of the timber and from the EXTREME SHARPNESS of the two curves, which carries much of the thrust down onto the potelet below the wall head. The madrier spandrel infill is a distinct part type (plank, rebated both edges). | VERIFICATION: verifier re-opened this plate and measured the half-truss at rise/run 563/288 px = 63 deg pitch (cross-checked on the plate's own 5 m bar at ~62 px/m: rise ~9.1 m, half-span ~4.65 m). This ENGLISH late-14th-c roof therefore sits inside the band the reader had reserved for France, and it is the single datum that kills the claimed France-vs-England pitch split. Text: 'La nef et les transsepts de la cathedrale d'Ely sont encore couverts par une belle charpente qui date de la fin du XIVe siecle.'

subject: Messina cathedral nave roof (Norman Sicily) - the basilican type with a coffered flat panel under the ridge
note: fig. 17 | DRAWING: perspective A and geometrical elevation B of one ferme | SEEN: A: perspective of one truss. An entrait of gigantic section set on edge, arbalétriers halved and pegged at the head with NO king-post, and a small richly coffered flat ceiling C under the ridge, hung from moises pendantes. Instead of purlins plus rafters, the chevrons are laid ACROSS (transversely) on the arbalétriers so they act as a dense ladder of small pannes; the drawing shows about twenty of them in one bay, each boxed by four nailed boards. B: geometrical elevation of the same, showing the low pitch and the corbel under the tie bearing. | FACTORY: Type-defining alternative to the French system - use it for 'southern / Norman-Sicilian / basilican' roofs: TIE_HEAVY_NO_KINGPOST + transverse rafter-ladder + double boarding + flat coffered panel under the ridge only. The dense transverse ladder is the reason the walls can be thin despite the low pitch: nothing is stacked outside the rafter plane.

subject: Reims cathedral nave roof, rebuilt late 15th / early 16th c - the fully dimensioned example
note: fig. 14 | DRAWING: transverse half-section plus two longitudinal sections (C on the axis through the king-posts, D on line A-B), 5 m scale bar | SEEN: Left: half transverse section, poinçon on the axis A-B, entrait at the bottom. Members labelled up the rafter: K (foot), H (poteau), G (contre-fiche), I (sous-arbalétriers-moises), E/F (the length of rafter carried on two panne courses), N (jambettes), O (collars), P and R (the two entraits retroussés of the ferme), S (jambettes), T (esseliers), D and P near the apex, U and V (two sous-faîtes). Right-hand longitudinal sections show croix de Saint-André between entretoises L and M and the very close spacing of the chevrons. No ironwork anywhere in the drawing. Geometry from the stated numbers (base 14.40, height 15.50) gives pitch 65.1 deg and a rafter hypotenuse of 17.09 m against the stated 17.00 m - the figure and the text agree. | FACTORY: THE reference ferme for a French late-Gothic cathedral: span 14.40, rise 15.50, pitch 65 deg, rafter 17.00, max scantling 0.22 m (= 8 pouces). Note the two-tier logic: the LOWER rafter length is carried on pannes fixed UNDER the arbalétrier (never on top), the UPPER length is stiffened only by jambettes and collars. So one roof has two different stiffening regimes along the same rafter - model it as a piecewise rule keyed to height. | VERIFICATION (pixel-measured, independent PNG decoder): the plate carries a graduated 5 m bar (x 92->386 px, five 58.8 px divisions = 58.8 px/m). Drawn half-truss: apex (29,61), rafter foot (452,972) -> half-base 423 px = 7.19 m (stated 7.20), rise 911 px = 15.49 m (stated 15.50), rafter 1004 px = 17.08 m (stated 17.00), pitch 65.1 deg; drawn poincon 13 px = 0.221 m = the stated 0.22 m / 8 pouces. So the whole stated triangle is independently confirmed and this is a true scaled drawing. CORRECTIONS to the reader: (a) section C is on the poincon axis and section D is on the dotted line A-B - they are TWO DIFFERENT planes 0.5-0.9 m apart, which is why both are drawn; the reader merged them. (b) the label the reader read as 'D' near the apex is 'O', the upper chevron collar. (c) the ferme's collars P and R lie 3.39 m and 6.09 m along the rafter from the head while the CHEVRON collars O lie at 2.66 m and 8.87 m - two distinct systems in two distinct planes, so the chevron bracing (jambettes N, collars O) must NOT be counted into the truss part list. (d) intervals 3.39 / 2.70 / 10.99 m are not equal: 'collars at equal intervals' is false for this truss.

subject: Sully-sur-Loire: longitudinal section showing the wind bracing and the dormers
note: fig. 27 | DRAWING: longitudinal section | SEEN: The whole length of the roof laid out. Two entretoises K run the length; between them a continuous row of croix de Saint-André L. Below and above them, great crossed écharpes M are lapped à tiers-bois on the OUTSIDE of the rafters, in the plane of the roof slope, running the full height of the roof and crossing in long diagonals. Lucarnes N sit in the width of two rafter intervals each. The chevrons are drawn very closely and uniformly spaced with no principals interrupting them. | FACTORY: Best wind-bracing figure in the article. Encode as two separate systems: (a) VERTICAL PLANE - St-Andrew crosses between longitudinal entretoises; (b) ROOF PLANE - crossed écharpes lapped at one third depth on the outside of the rafters, with fourrures (packing pieces) laid over the rafters to make up the resulting step before the boarding goes on. Viollet says it is chiefly (b) that stops the roof rolling. Dormer width = 2 rafter bays = about 1.26 m at 0.63 m spacing.

subject: Grand'salle of the château of Sully-sur-Loire, late 14th c: transverse section
note: fig. 26 | DRAWING: transverse section with figures for scale, plus detail X of the wall-walk roof, 5 m / 10 m scale bar | SEEN: Full transverse section from the Loire side (left) to the courtyard (right). A pointed lambris barrel fills the hall; ABOVE it the chevrons continue to the ridge, braced by a small triangulated frame with a St-Andrew cross at collar level. There are NO ties and NO principal rafters at all: only chevrons portant ferme, and even those have no poinçons. Floor beams A (with stone corbels B) do the tie's work. Sablière C on corbels/wall head, second sablière D above carrying jambettes E that curve at their heads into the chevrons. Blochets P drawn as PAIRS of moises gripping jambette and rafter foot into the outer sablière R. Outside the hall wall, big coyaux G stiffened by small curved contrefiches H roof the machicolated wall-walks (detail X, top left). Two figures are drawn standing on the floor for scale. Eyeball pitch is very steep, about 68-70 deg. | FACTORY: Type: MILITARY GREAT HALL, no truss at all. Full dimension set in the text (see dimensions[]). Two things to encode: (1) the FLOOR BEAM IS THE TIE ('les entraits de cette charpente ne sont, par le fait, que les énormes poutres transversales du plancher') - so a hall roof may legitimately have no entrait if the floor below is framed; (2) the wall-walk is roofed by a separate small pointed barrel of coyaux outside the hall wall, which is a distinctive castle silhouette. | VERIFICATION: pitch measures ~68 deg - the steepest French roof in the article.

subject: Conical roof: perspective of the second enrayure towards the circumference, with four joint details
note: fig. 36 bis | DRAWING: perspective construction/assemblage detail + separate part drawings | SEEN: Perspective looking down on the second enrayure. Courbes/esseliers A under the arbalétriers B of the two principal fermes relieve the coyers D and are clamped to rafter and coyer by small moises C C tightened by the key F. Chevrons E are likewise gripped by moises tying them to the courbes. Their bending is stopped by coyers G tenoned into goussets H. Linçoirs I (trimmers) are tenoned between the chevrons and receive the heads of the faux chevrons K, expressly so that erection is possible. Separate part drawings I', I'', I''' show the linçoir with its shouldered tenons, and C/F show a moise pair with its key. | FACTORY: Gives the ERECTION ORDER for a cone, which Viollet says is the real difficulty (all pieces converge on one axis, so tenons must be enterable): circular sablières -> the two right-angle fermes raised and assembled -> goussets -> chevrons with their coyers and esseliers -> linçoirs -> faux chevrons, all going in from OUTSIDE INWARD without lifting the principal trusses again. Encode this as a hard constraint on any procedural cone: secondary members must be insertable radially.

subject: Conical roof of a cylindrical tower: circular plan, one quadrant per enrayure level
note: fig. 35 | DRAWING: plan (four quadrants at four different levels) | SEEN: Circle divided into quadrants by the two crossing entraits E-F and G-H, with the central poinçon I at the crossing. Quadrant A (top right) = the low enrayure at sablière level: six radial chevrons per quadrant whose prolonged blochets form the enrayure by tenoning into a large gousset M, with lighter faux chevrons between them landing on ordinary blochets. Quadrant B = the second enrayure, C = the third, D = the horizontal projection at the top level. The ring of double circular sablières is drawn at the perimeter. The radial density visibly halves as the levels rise (the faux chevrons stop at the second enrayure). | FACTORY: Direct generator spec for a tower cone: N_quadrants=4, chevrons_per_quadrant=6 (24 total), faux chevrons interleaved only between enrayure 1 and 2, 2 crossing entraits at 90 deg, central poinçon, 3+ enrayure rings, double circular sablière ring. Key structural note from the text: conical roofs often have NO ties at the base at all - the circular sablières, strongly keyed together, resist the rafter thrust 'comme le ferait un cercle d'une seule pièce'. A keyed ring beam is the hoop tie.

subject: Very large truss: contre-fiche additionally carrying esseliers and liens that relieve the principal rafter
note: fig. 16 | DRAWING: perspective construction/assemblage detail | SEEN: Perspective from below/outside. The hatched field is the underside of the rafters/boarding. A contre-fiche rises to a panne; from its head an esselier and a lien splay out to pick up the arbalétrier on either side, all housed and pegged, forming a rigid triangulated node. Members are lightly moulded/chamfered. | FACTORY: Escalation rule: as span grows, the contre-fiche node acquires (1) goussets to the panne, then (2) esseliers and liens back to the rafter. Viollet also credits this gusset-into-panne family with stopping the HIEMENT of trusses and rafters, i.e. it is the wind-bracing as well as the load path.

subject: The canonical French seating of a 13th-c roof on a narrow bahut - double sablière, entrait, blochet, jambette
note: fig. 7 | DRAWING: perspective assembly detail plus part-plan and three joint details | SEEN: Perspective looking along the wall head. A = the stone bahut. Two named parameters fall out: jambette_rake (vertical for very steep roofs, raked for shallower - 'plus les combles sont aigus, plus les jambettes se rapprochent de la verticale'), and the optional horizontal pieces H between the plates at mid-bay which carry rafter thrust back to the fixed dovetail points.

subject: Auxerre great hall: one chevron portant ferme (a common rafter framed as a truss)

Viollet's stated reason for the crossed contre-fiches is explicitly wind and asymmetric load ('elles empêchent le triangle de se déformer par l'action du vent ou d'une charge plus forte d'un côté que de l'autre') - so cross-bracing in the truss plane is an ASYMMETRIC-LOAD device, distinct from longitudinal St-Andrew crosses.

subject: Roof over a pointed barrel vault: the false-tie problem (Autun, Beaune, Saulieu type)
note: fig. 6 | DRAWING: transverse section (labelled COVPE for the longitudinal section at left) with 0-5 m scale bar | SEEN: Right: a pointed barrel vault (berceau tiers-point) drawn in section with the roof frame sitting on it. The cornice of the gutter walls is at A, well BELOW the crown of the vault at B, so no tie can pass. Options (a) and (b) are FAILURE MODES: Viollet says both eventually spread.

subject: fig.5 — corbelled steps (escalier en encorbellement), tour d'Orange, Carpentras (early XIV c.)
note: fig. 5 | DRAWING: detail: single-block trace A, perspective G, elevation H, profile K, with a 1 m bar | SEEN: A single step block is drawn at A with the tail B destined to be built into the wall and points c and D marked; the perspective G shows the blocks laid so that point C of one falls on point D of the next, producing a stepped series of corbelled retreats with deeply undercut (scooped) soffits; the elevation H shows the run bedded into coursed ashlar; K is the profile. subject: fig.6 — 45-degree stair with wedge (coin) steps
note: fig. 6 | DRAWING: plan, elevation on ab, perspective C | SEEN: Plan at top left shows a run of triangular treads alternating apex left/right, dimensioned 0,30 between the two flanking lines; the elevation top right is dimensioned 0,30 c. for the rise of a pair; perspective C shows a booted pair of legs standing with one foot on tread A and the other on tread B, the treads wedge-shaped so each is 0,30 wide at one end and nothing at the other. | FACTORY: Type WEDGE_STEP_45_DEGREE (service/fortification only). Viollet's reason: only one foot is ever on a step at a time, so full tread width is wasted. | VERIFICATION: the '0,30' arrow lies HORIZONTALLY along the line a-b, spanning one cell, and the companion drawing is lettered 'Elevat. sur a.b' with '0,30 c.' as a VERTICAL dimension spanning two rises - which proves a-b is the direction of ascent. subject: fig.7 — vis with helical barrel vault, XI-XII c.
note: fig. 7 | DRAWING: coupe (upper) + plan (lower), section on line AB of the plan | SEEN: Section shows the round tower shaft: rubble base, then coursed ashlar, the helical vault visible in section with the newel drums bearing an epaulement H on one side and the vault courses notched into the circular wall I on the other; two round-arched embrasures. Plan: black wall mass, thin circular cage face, small solid black newel at the centre, 18 radial treads; the outer door is at D (lower right, splayed passage through the wall), the first step at C (the horizontal radial to the east, which is also the section line), G marks where the solid fill (massif) ends and the spiral vault begins (lower left). A curved arrow with a hatched tail glyph in the upper right shows the direction of ascent. MEASURED on the plate: 18 radial treads per full revolution = 20.0 deg per step (radii 55/70/85 px all give 18 evenly spaced lines); newel radius 18.5 px, cage inner radius 94.5 px, so newel diameter = 0.196 x cage internal diameter; scaling by Viollet's stated 1,90 m cage gives newel 0.37 m, tread net 0.76 m, matching his stated 'au moins un pied' and '0,80 c. au plus'. ARROW GEOMETRY: tail at 28 deg, head at 67 deg (measured from centre 182.5, 818) => ascent is COUNTER-CLOCKWISE in plan. | FACTORY: Type VIS_ON_HELICAL_BARREL (earliest medieval). Assembly order: (1) build round tower shaft; (2) raise newel as stacked drums, each with an epaulement to receive the vault springer; (3) bed the low steps on solid fill up to point G; (4) turn the helical barrel of small rubble on couchis, springing off the newel epaulements and notched into the cage wall; (5) lay the stone steps on the extrados of the barrel, arrises on the radii of the circle. Parameters: cage internal dia (1.90 m nominal), newel dia = 0.20 x cage dia, 18 winders/turn. | VERIFICATION: 18 radial treads confirmed independently, mean gap 20.0 deg (two spurious minima caused by the ascent arrow itself discarded). Ascent arrow re-measured counter-clockwise: tail 31 deg -> head 70 deg about newel centroid (183.8, 816.2).

subject: fig.8 — newel drum cut to receive the helical vault springers, abbey church of Eu (XII c.)
note: fig. 8 | DRAWING: perspective detail | SEEN: A single cylindrical newel drum with a helical seating cut around it: a flat sloping ledge sweeping up around the drum with a raised fillet, leaving a spiral shoulder for the vault voussoirs. Vertical tooling/hatching over the barrel. | FACTORY: Newel drum primitive: cylinder + helical sweep cut. Viollet notes the alternative (notching the vault bearings straight into the plain cylinder) badly weakens the newel, so the cut-shoulder drum is the better version. One reusable Blender operation: helical boolean/sweep on a cylinder, parametrised by pitch = riser and by shoulder depth.

subject: fig.9 — vis with each step carrying a piece of the newel (from early XIII c.)
note: fig. 9 | DRAWING: coupe + plan + perspective detail C + step profile D | SEEN: Perspective C at left shows one step: a wedge-shaped slab whose inner end swells into a rounded segment of the newel; D below is the step seen from beneath with the chamfered (delarde) underside indicated by a dotted line. The section at right (taken on ab but 'en pourtournant le noyau', i.e. developed around the newel, per footnote 7) shows the steps stacked with their newel-blocks and their overlaps; the polygonal outer mass is hatched. Plan bottom right: hatched wall, hatched newel, radial steps, the exterior door at A (lower right, cut through the canted mass) and the first step at B (the east radial); dotted lines in the upper right quadrant are the recouvrements (the overlap of the following step). MEASURED: centre (367, 678), cage radius 110 px, newel radius approx. 21 px => newel/cage = 0.19 (same ratio as fig.7); step spacing 19.5-20.5 deg => 18 winders per revolution. | FACTORY: Type VIS_MONOLITHIC_STEP_WITH_NEWEL_BLOCK — the workhorse. Each step is ONE stone = wedge tread + integral newel drum segment + a bearing notched a few cm into the cage wall. Steps overlap slightly (mordre l'une sur l'autre). Generator consequence: a single parametric step mesh, instanced 18x per turn with a 20 deg rotation and one riser of Z; no vault, no centring. The steps themselves tie newel to cage (etresillons), so the cage wall can be thin. | VERIFICATION: 18 winders confirmed, mean gap 20.0 deg.

subject: fig.10 — Viollet's reconstruction of the grande vis of Charles V's Louvre (Raymond du Temple, 1365), ground-floor plan
note: fig. 10 | DRAWING: plan, with a 0-15 m scale bar | SEEN: A free-standing circular stair tower. Centre: a large hollow newel drawn as a thick dark ring, opened north and south by a rectangular rib-vaulted passage so that at ground level one walks straight through from the portico C to the north range B. Left half of the circle shows the rib vaults under the flight (keystones marked at F top and E bottom, springing G); right half shows the radial winders. Ten buttresses H stand round the outside (counted: 10, matching the ten statue niches Sauval describes). A at bottom is the junction with the north range, C at top the portico carrying the gallery to the donjon, D the first step, B an arrow leaving the plan. MEASURED against the plate's own scale bar (ticks at 0/5/10/15 m give 29.55 px per m): newel outer diameter 115 px = 3.89 m, newel ring wall 31 px = 1.05 m, central void 45 px = 1.52 m, cage internal radius 125 px = 4.23 m (internal diameter 8.46 m). Step length = 125-58 = 67 px = 2.27 m, which is EXACTLY Sauval's stated 'sept pieds de longueur'. Winder spacing measured at radii 80/95/110 px = 9.7 deg => about 37 winders per revolution. | FACTORY: CONJECTURAL RESTORATION — Viollet says so explicitly. Still the single richest parametric target: GRAND_VIS_HORS_D_OEUVRE. Generator: circular tower set entirely outside the ranges, tied in only by a landing; hollow newel large enough (a) to carry a second smaller vis above and (b) to be walked through at ground level; buttress count = statue count = 10; landings carried on rib vaults or pierced arches because no single stone could span them. | VERIFICATION: scale bar confirmed at 29.6 px/m (major ticks y=153/301/448/597 = 15/10/5/0 m); 10 buttresses confirmed by count; winders re-measured at ~36 per revolution against the reader's 37 (inside noise). Viollet states outright that this is not a survey: 'Nous ne pretendons pas ... presenter ces figures comme un releve scrupuleux de ce monument detruit depuis le XVIIe siecle, et dont il ne reste aucun dessin.'

subject: fig.11 — the same, section on line CB
note: fig. 11 | DRAWING: coupe, with a 0-10 m scale bar | SEEN: Tall section: the ground-level arcade with mounted figures under it, then three storeys of the adjoining range at the right with vaulted rooms and traceried windows, the stair cage at the centre showing the successive revolutions of the flight and the landings level with each floor, the pierced/openwork newel structure, K marking the level of the last landing of the great vis from which the small vis rises inside arcatures ressautantes (stepped arcading), and above that a crowning lantern with a spire, crocketed pinnacles, a terrace balustrade with fleurs-de-lis cresting, and a statue on a pinnacle. Graduated bar 0-10 m at the base. | FACTORY: CONJECTURAL. Encodes the vertical rules: landings must be de plain-pied with the floors of the adjoining range; a smaller vis continues from the top landing to the terrace inside the cage of the greater, lit through the great cage by stepped arcading; a lantern crowns the whole and gives access to the terrace.

subject: fig.12 — perspective taken beneath the upper landing of the same
note: fig. 12 | DRAWING: perspective | SEEN: Looking up into the stair: openwork tracery arches carry the landing overhead, the raking soffit of the steps visible above, two traceried doorways off the landing, a large canted statue on a corbel with a dais at the right, a lady descending at the left and a servant standing in the doorway. Wall is fine ashlar with narrow lancets. | FACTORY: CONJECTURAL. Useful for the interior read: landings are supported by pierced arches (arcs ajoures) not by single slabs; the doorways off a vis landing can be multiple and set at an angle to each other; sculpture is carried on corbels that ressaut with the helix.

subject: fig.13 — Viollet's plan explaining Sauval's double-newel double-revolution vis at the Bernardins, Paris (begun 1336)
note: fig. 13 | DRAWING: plan | SEEN: An OVAL (two-centred) cage, hatched. Two hatched newels, one in the upper half and one in the lower, joined by a straight neck. The upper half's winders radiate from the upper newel, the lower half's from the lower newel; solid lines for one flight, dashed for the other. A and B are the two entrances at left and right on a dashed horizontal, C and D the two first steps, E the middle zone. Two curved arrows with hatched tails. MEASURED (upper arrow, newel centre approx. 197, 189): tail at 28 deg, head at 51 deg => COUNTER-CLOCKWISE ascent. | FACTORY: CONJECTURE — Viollet writes 'En cherchant a expliquer par une figure la description de Sauval, on trouverait le plan (13)'. Type DOUBLE_VIS_TWO_NEWELS: two interleaved helices in one cage, each flight passing over the other, two doors, two occupants who can neither meet nor see each other. Generator: pitch of each flight = 2 x giron; the two helices are offset 180 deg in phase. | VERIFICATION: both ascent arrows re-measured counter-clockwise (upper tail 27 -> 53 deg, lower tail 214 -> 238 deg). Viollet's plates therefore disagree with each other on handedness - figs 7 and 13 counter-clockwise, fig 15 clockwise - which is itself the evidence that he did not treat handedness as a rule.

subject: fig.14 — stair tower of the chateau de Gaillon (first years of XVI c.)
note: fig. 14 | DRAWING: plan | SEEN: An octagonal stair tower set in the re-entrant angle of two porticoes E and F. Heavy black buttresses/piers at the octagon angles. Two outer arches A A give entry from outside, two arches B B give entry from under the portico; D is the first step; G is the opening in the angle by which the upper storeys enter the galleries. The newel is a small circle drawn as a clustered/ringed shaft. Radial winders fill the octagon. | FACTORY: Type VIS_IN_RE_ENTRANT_ANGLE, hors d'oeuvre. Generator rule extracted: putting the tower in the angle between two ranges lets you open FOUR doors at ground level (two exterior, two into the portico) and, at each upper level, one door through the angle into the galleries — and it disturbs no interior distribution at all.

subject: fig.15 — vis in a SQUARE cage with corner trompes, XV c.
note: fig. 15 | DRAWING: plan | SEEN: Square cage, black walls. Large dark newel at the centre with a ring (the bandeau/cornice) around it. A circle is inscribed in the square: the cylinder within which the treads giron. Radial treads: on the left half all solid; on the right half alternating solid and dashed (the revolution above). C labels the first step on the south radial; E marks the entry; below the cage a rib-vaulted portico A-B with round piers. A curved arrow with a hatched tail lies at the lower left. MEASURED: newel radius approx. 21 px, cage inner face approx. 130 px, step spacing 13.3 deg => about 27 winders per revolution; taking the companion section's scale (59.4 px/m) gives cage internal 4.3 m, newel 0.71 m, tread 1.80 m, giron at the wall 0.50 m. ARROW GEOMETRY: tail at 251 deg, head at 226 deg (centre 279.5, 187.5) => ascent is CLOCKWISE — the OPPOSITE hand to figs 7 and 13. | FACTORY: Type VIS_IN_SQUARE_CAGE_WITH_TROMPES. Generator: square cage; the treads giron in the inscribed cylinder so all treads are the same length and all delardees the same way; the four corners are filled by trompes (squinches) rising to a spiral cornice, and only the corner treads are longer. Payoff Viollet states: users get the whole square cage, but the masons still cut one repeated tread. Bigger cage => more winders per turn (27 here vs 18 in the small early vis). | VERIFICATION: 27 winders per turn at ~13.4 deg CONFIRMED, tread 1.80 m confirmed, and the clockwise ascent arrow confirmed (tail ~282 deg -> head ~224 deg, cross-checked by the dotted-tread convention). REFUTED: newel diameter is 0.92-0.95 m (filled disc r=24 px with its bandeau outline at r~27-28, so 54-56 px at 59 px/m), not 0.71 m; cage internal is 4.47 m square (inner faces x=147 and x=411, newel centre 278.4, symmetric to 1.2 px), not 4.2-4.3 m. Scale-free the ratio also disagrees: 0.205 measured against 0.165 claimed. Recomputed giron at the wall: 2*pi*2.235/27 = 0.52 m, so the reader's 0.50 m survives.

subject: fig.16 — section of fig.15 on line AB
note: fig. 16 | DRAWING: coupe, drawn in three stacked registers, with a 0-4 m scale bar | SEEN: The tall section is broken into three horizontal strips to fit the page: bottom = ground/portico level with the doorway into the stair and the raking soffit of the first revolution, middle = arrival G at the entresol, top = arrival H at the first floor with a standing figure. Turned/pierced balustrades rake with each flight; moulded spiral cornices; two-centred arches over the arrivals; the helical soffit of the flight is drawn sweeping across the openings. MEASURED: scale ticks at 1 m intervals give 59.4 px/m; cage internal width approx. 247 px = 4.16 m; each register approx. 250 px = 4.2 m of height. If one revolution serves one 4.2 m level at 27 winders, the riser is about 0.155 m, inside Viollet's stated 0.15-0.20 m band. | FACTORY: Confirms the vertical parameters for the square-cage vis: arrivals at portico, entresol (G) and first floor (H); balustrade at every flight; storey approx. 4.2 m. Use with fig.15 as the matched plan/section pair for the generator. | VERIFICATION: scale bar confirmed at 59.0 px/m (major ticks x=72/130/188.5/249/308 with '2' and '4 m' labels) against the reader's 59.4.

subject: fig.17 — view at the level of the first revolution, chateau de Chateaudun
note: fig. 17 | DRAWING: perspective | SEEN: Taken where the first revolution cuts the ground-floor portico in its height. Shows the corner trompes as slightly inclined jointed plates-bandes, foliate culs-de-lampe at the octagon angles, the moulded SPIRAL CORNICE with a beaded/billet enrichment running round and carrying the outer ends of the steps, the underside of the steps delarde (dressed off) into a smooth raking soffit above, a pierced balustrade with quatrefoil-and-mouchette panels, and coursed ashlar behind. | FACTORY: Verified assembly for the large square-cage vis: square -> octagon via appareilles trompes -> culs-de-lampe at the octagon angles -> spiral cornice whose horizontal projection is a perfect circle -> step ends bear on that cornice. That is the load path a generator must reproduce; the cornice is the ring that converts a square cage into a circular stair.

subject: fig.18 — horizontal projection of the same
note: fig. 18 | DRAWING: plan | SEEN: Square hatched cage; the corners cut by trompes drawn as arcs with small circles at the angle points; a large true circle inscribed (the spiral cornice, whose horizontal projection is a perfect circle) filling almost the whole square; a small circle at the dead centre = the newel; three thickened bases at the bottom and a small dark segment at the bottom centre (the doorway). | FACTORY: The diagnostic drawing for the type: the cornice circle is tangent to the square, and the newel is small relative to it. Generator: newel radius approx. 1/5 of the cornice radius on this plate — much slenderer than the fig.15 example, so newel diameter is NOT a fixed fraction across the XV c. group.

subject: fig.19 — trompillon from the hotel de la Tremoille, Paris (demolished 1840)
note: fig. 19 | DRAWING: perspective + small plan inset | SEEN: A corner squinch carved from a single stone: a large fluted shell/palmette flanked by curling acanthus, under a heavy moulded spiral cornice which carries the raking step soffits above (their undersides shown as smooth rakes). Ashlar pier below with vertical tooling. A small plan inset at the lower right shows the corner triangle with its radial ribs. | FACTORY: Type TROMPILLON: for smaller square-cage vis the corner is a single carved stone (one gousset), not a jointed trompe. Viollet adds the functional detail: these corner pockets are where the torches went — on small culs-de-lampe, in little niches, or on iron brackets sealed into the wall. That is a light-source placement rule for a game.

subject: fig.20 — a piece of the newel of the Chateaudun vis
note: fig. 20 | DRAWING: elevation detail | SEEN: A tall segment of newel built in high courses (assises hautes), its face covered with delicate foliate ornament set in two tall panels under trefoiled arches, with vase-and-stem motifs. A = the main-courante (handrail) worked in the solid of the newel and running helically; B = the bandeau (spiral fillet) receiving the inner ends of the steps, with the incrustement (housing) of the steps indicated. The raking soffits of the steps sweep across the top left and bottom right; small stepped blocks show where each tread beds in. | FACTORY: Newel primitive for the grand XV c. vis: cylinder in tall courses + helical handrail moulding cut in the solid + helical bandeau with step housings. Two helices at the same pitch (riser), different radius and profile. Fragments of the Tremoille newel survive at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts (Viollet's footnote). | VERIFICATION: re-opened. The sheet is lettered A on the upper roll moulding and B on the moulded band beneath the housed step ends, matching 'En A est la main-courante, et en B le bandeau recevant les marches'. The two-helices-at-one-pitch reading is consistent with the woodcut.

subject: fig.21 — vis with NO newel (from XIV c., for very tight spaces)
note: fig. 21 | DRAWING: perspective G + coupe B on CD + plan A | SEEN: G: one step in perspective, a wedge slab whose inner end swells into a rounded boudin (roll) that forms the handrail, with the delarde underside dotted. B: section against coursed ashlar showing four or five steps simply superposed in a spiral, their boudins stacking into a continuous roll and the soffits scooped. A: half-plan, radial treads converging on a RING of boudins around an open void (no newel at all), the outer wall hatched. MEASURED: step spacing at radii 80/100 px = 20.5 deg => about 18 winders per revolution; the open jour is roughly 12 per cent of the cage diameter. | FACTORY: Type VIS_SANS_NOYAU. Generator: identical tread instancing to the standard vis, but the inner end terminates in a boudin instead of a newel block, and the axis is a void. Viollet's stated reason: it frees the centre for the people passing, which is what you want when the cage is tiny. The stacked boudins ARE the handrail — no separate rail geometry needed. | VERIFICATION: half-plan gives 8 interior radials + 2 boundaries = 9 sectors x 20.2 deg = 18 per turn. Confirmed.

subject: fig.22 — open (ajouree) vis enclosed by colonnettes, Mainz cathedral (mid XIII c.)
note: fig. 22 | DRAWING: elevation of one whole revolution + half-plan, with a 2 m dimension arrow | SEEN: Elevation: a helix of steps, each step's outer end carried by its own slender colonnette with base, shaft and foliate/Corinthianesque capital, all the colonnettes of equal height, so the capitals climb in a helix; the steps carry the newel; behind, coursed and rubble masonry rises only to level A. Half-plan below: outer arc, nine colonnette shafts drawn as circles with dark cores, radial treads, a small dark newel at the centre. MEASURED against the plate's own 2 m arrow (334 px = 2 m, so 167 px/m): outer radius 168 px = 1.01 m (outer diameter approx. 2.0 m); newel radius approx. 25 px => newel diameter approx. 0.30 m (one pied); tread length approx. 0.85 m; radial spacing at radii 60/75/90/105 px = 20.4 deg => 18 winders per revolution; the repeating step-course spacing in the elevation is 27.2 px = 0.163 m, i.e. the riser is about 0.16 m (half a pied); one revolution therefore rises about 2.9 m. | FACTORY: Type VIS_AJOUREE_ON_COLONNETTES — the fully parametric case, and the ONLY plate in the article from which riser, going, newel and diameter can all be measured. 'Rien n'est plus simple et plus elegant.' Generator: above level A there is no wall at all; the structure is (step carrying newel segment) + (one colonnette per step, all identical). Instance count 18 per turn, 20 deg, 0.163 m rise. | VERIFICATION REFUTES four of the reader's six numbers on the plate it called 'the fully determined vis' and 'the reference instance'. CONFIRMED: scale 167 px/m from the plate's own dimension arrow (tips y=210 and y=544 = 334 px, label read at 8x as '2 m 00'); tread length 142 px = 0.85 m; riser ~0.16 m (consecutive colonnette abaci at y 645/620/596/566/539, mean 26.5 px = 0.159 m). REFUTED: colonnettes in the half-plan are EIGHT, not nine (re-rendered as two 5x quarter crops, 4+4, centres at x = 92, 109, 140, 186, 237, 288, 324, 346); winders per revolution are SIXTEEN at 22.5 deg, not eighteen at 20.4 - the half-plan has exactly 7 interior radials at 202.0/225.0/247.5/270.0/294.0/317.0/339.0 from centre (219.8, 797.0), which with the two diameter ends gives 8 sectors whose gaps (22.0/23.0/22.5/22.5/24.0/23.0/22.0/21.0) sum to exactly 180.0, and one colonnette per step is what the text requires ('des colonnettes ... soutenant chacune l'extremite exterieure d'une marche'); the newel is 0.17 m in diameter (black semicircle r=14.2 px, half-widths 14.0/11.5/6.0 at dy 3/8/13 below the diameter line y=797), not 0.30 m - so the rhetorical clincher 'almost exactly the un pied minimum Viollet states' is fabricated, and this vis in fact has a newel about HALF his stated minimum, which is the genuinely interesting datum for a light open tower vis; outer diameter is 1.87 m (outer arc x 63.5->375.5 = 312 px, r=156 px), not 2.00 m; rise per revolution is therefore ~2.55-2.61 m, not 2.9 m. The newel/outer-diameter ratio fails even scale-free: 0.089 measured against 0.15 claimed.

subject: fig.23 — vis in the tower pinnacles of Reims cathedral
note: fig. 23 | DRAWING: perspective of one block | SEEN: One enormous block cut as THREE steps in a single course, its inner end forming the newel D as a bulbous shaft; the outer ends of the treads are relieved by separate stones set in delit: slender stone chandelles B rise as posts, their tops A supporting the tread bearings and then re-appearing over the step ends at C. The stone is stippled. | FACTORY: Type VIS_MULTI_STEP_MONOLITH (only where the quarry yields huge blocks). Generator: step count per course becomes a parameter (3 at Reims). Viollet's structural reading matters: the newel D carries the entire load and the chandelles B are only a series of props forming an open screen — so they can be slender and are not a load path.

subject: fig.24 — covering a wide stair inside a massive wall with juxtaposed arches
note: fig. 24 | DRAWING: elevations A and A-prime, coupe B, trace D, coupe E | SEEN: A = a pointed (brise) arch and A-prime = a semicircular arch, each drawn as a series of concentric voussoir rings in ashlar, all springing from the same nu (face); c marks the springer level. D at the left is a stack of corbelled blocks in elevation; B (bottom right) is the raking flight itself, covered by a series of lintels stepped up the rake with corbels under each bearing, with a man-at-arms with a polearm on the steps for scale; E (bottom left) shows the same construction in coarse rubble. | FACTORY: Type COVERED_RAKING_PASSAGE. Two variants and the stated reasons: (1) WIDE flights are covered by a series of arches juxtaposed and stepped up the rake — all springings on one nu, all arches cut to the SAME curve, so the springers are equally bedded and you avoid the long tracing, heavy stone waste and delicate setting of a true raking barrel; and stepped arches do not let the construction above slide, which a raking barrel can. (2) NARROW flights get a series of lintels stepped up the rake, relieved by corbels at the bearings. Both are cheap to generate: one arch mesh, or one lintel mesh, translated along the rake.

subject: fig.25 — the same lintelled covering with a continuous moulded profile
note: fig. 25 | DRAWING: perspective | SEEN: Looking up a raking passage: instead of separate corbels, a broad continuous moulding ressauts at right angles at each covering stone, so the soffit reads as a stepped moulded band; the flight's steps and the ashlar cheeks are drawn beneath. | FACTORY: The decorative variant of fig.24 D/E: 'D'une necessite de construction ces architectes ont fait ici, comme partout, un motif de decoration.' Generator: replace the discrete corbel with a swept profile that steps at each lintel — one profile curve plus a stepping path.

subject: fig.26 — elements of a straight wooden flight: the limon
note: fig. 26 | DRAWING: perspective A, section B, log-conversion diagram | SEEN: A: the inner face of a straight limon (string) with the steps housed into it, their front ends rounded; c, D, E mark the tenon, the epaulement and the embrevement; G are the balustrade posts standing on the limon, H the renforts (thickened blocks) mortised to receive them. B (right) is the limon in section with c and D again. Middle: the limon and step in perspective from beneath, showing the delarde underside forming a raking soffit. Bottom: a circle = the end of an oak log, divided by three saw cuts (I-I lines, plus L) into six triangles, each containing one wavy step profile, with M marking the leftover dosses. | FACTORY: Type TIMBER_STRAIGHT_FLIGHT. Steps are always SOLID (pleines), tenoned and mortised into the limon, and delardees beneath to form a raking soffit — there are no contremarches in medieval work. The log diagram is a manufacturing rule worth keeping: 0.50 m oak log, 3 saw cuts, 6 triangles, 1 step each, front of step toward the heart because that is the face that wears, sapwood and flaches end up in the tail, and the cuts follow the direction of the shakes so the step cannot check or warp.

subject: fig.27 — wooden stair of two flights with landings, straight limons and corner posts
note: fig. 27 | DRAWING: plan A (1:100) + longitudinal coupe on ab (1:50), with a 0-2 m bar | SEEN: Plan (top): rectangular hatched cage; the two flights flank a narrow well; four black corner posts; B = first step, C = first landing, D = second flight's first step, E = the landing at first-floor level. Section (below): four corner posts rising from a stone parpaing, limons framed into them, the marche palière G halved into post F and further relieved by a poutrelle tenoned onto the renfort H, gousset I and a long lien K under the third flight, a turned balustrade with rail framed into the posts, a pierced trefoil panel in the triangle between post, limon and lien; a robed man with a staff at the lower left for scale; L marks the detailed junction. MEASURED against the bar (58.8 px/m): cage internally about 3.16 m x 4.68 m; the well between the flights about 1.0 m; posts spaced 0.99 m across and 2.30 m along. | FACTORY: Type TIMBER_TWO_FLIGHT_WITH_LANDINGS — 'l'escalier de charpente le plus simple'. Generator skeleton: 4 posts running from foundation to head, limons framed post-to-post, one marche palière per landing halved into the post, poutrelle + gousset + lien as the stiffening set. Viollet's reason for the liens: they stop the roulement and poussees a multi-storey timber stair develops, and the pierced panel in the triangle stiffens the whole frame. He notes this system lasted to the XVII c. and does NOT sag the way modern strings attached only to landing treads do.

subject: fig.28 — the joints: limons into posts, landing treads, thrust beams
note: fig. 28 | DRAWING: perspective details + dimensioned projection A | SEEN: Top: the marche palière Q in perspective with tenons U, V, X and the peg hole Y. Left: the post in perspective (O) with N the renfort for the poutrelle de buttee, P the two mortises and the embrevement, R the housing for the landing tread with the bolt hole S, T the gousset — drawn as a slender post with a splayed foliate stop. Right: projection A with the two facing posts, DIMENSIONED 0,20c across and 0,18 (ringed) the other way; the arriving and departing limons E-E-prime and F-F-prime, the gousset D, the poutrelle C with its double tenon and its profile C-prime, the landing tread K with its bolt M, and the bolt holes; B at the bottom is the post continuing down. | FACTORY: The dimensions on the plate CONFIRM the text: posts 0,18 x 0,20 m, set on edge in the direction of the emmarchement; limons 0,15 m thick, flush with the OUTER face of the posts (not centred on them). The landing tread is halved into the post, part-borne on the poutrelle, and drawn up tight by a bolt through the gousset. Everything is visible joinery and IS the decoration.

subject: fig.29 — wooden vis with two newels and two flights
note: fig. 29 | DRAWING: plan | SEEN: Oval hatched cage. At the centre two newels B B drawn as a rounded double form joined by two crossing limons. C-prime at the left and C at the right are the two doors. A (upper) and A (lower) are the two first steps. Solid radial lines are one flight, dashed the other, the two gironning one above the other. | FACTORY: Type TIMBER_DOUBLE_VIS. Steps are debillardees and solid, tenoned at the inner end into BOTH newels and into the limons, and at the outer end either built into the masonry or borne on a filet (fillet) nailed along a pan de bois. Viollet: these were very common through to the XVII c. and 'on ne s'explique pas pourquoi on a cesse de les mettre en oeuvre'. The two doors let two households share one shaft without meeting.

subject: fig.30 — joinery vis: step, montants, newel blocks, bolt
note: fig. 30 | DRAWING: perspective M + elevation G + plan A + details O, N, P | SEEN: Top (M): one step in perspective — front elege at S, visible about T, two notches Q where the montants pass and embreve, the gousset tongue housing beneath, and the rear debillardement V. Middle (G): elevation of a quarter of the circumference showing the montants as tall posts, the step abouts K bearing on goussets J embreved into the montants, I the bolt threading the newel blocks, K/L the scooped step undersides; N is the gousset alone, P and R details, b-prime the tongue. Bottom left (A): fan plan with the newel C at the apex (drawn as a ring = the bolt) and seven black montants B round the arc, steps A and B labelled, dashed lines E and F giving the recouvrement. Bottom right (O): horizontal section of a montant at 1/10 full size, with a and b the tenon and the gousset embrevement. | FACTORY: Type JOINERY_VIS (Sainte-Chapelle sacraire, XIII c.; tour Saint-Romain, Rouen, XV c.). STATED: 12 steps per circumference (30 deg per step). Each step carries its own newel block; a round iron rod/bolt threads all the blocks and stops them deviating; one montant per step, one piece per storey, tenoned at the foot into a plateau and at the head into a cercle — so the cage is a prism with as many faces as there are steps. Apart from the axis bolt there is NO ironwork. Entry: two montants cut off 2 m above the floor and carried on a traverse framed into the neighbouring posts. | VERIFICATION: the reader's 'seven black montants B round the arc' is wrong - there are SIX (centroids x = 46.7, 97.4, 165.4, 243.4, 311.5, 360.9; angles 215.3/236.6/258.5/281.9/304.0/325.6 about a fitted centre 203.8, 792.8, with no gap for a seventh). NEW FINDING: this plate CONTRADICTS the article's only stated steps-per-turn figure. The text says 'le plan d'un quart d'un escalier de ce genre portant douze marches sur sa circonference' (12/turn = 30 deg, so a quarter should show 3 steps), but plan A draws 5 steps between 6 montants spanning 110 deg, i.e. ~22 deg each and ~16 per turn, and is not a quarter. Keep 12 as the quoted statement; do not use it as a verified timber-vis parameter without noting the plate says otherwise.

subject: fig.31 — newel of the joinery vis of the college de Montaigu, Paris (demolished, seen by Viollet)
note: fig. 31 | DRAWING: elevation detail + profiles D and E | SEEN: A turned newel worked from a single timber as a column with two TWISTED ribs (nervures torses) winding round it. A = the mortises for the steps, stepping up the helix; B = the epaulement below each mortise to relieve the bearing; C = the main courante worked in the solid; D = the handrail profile cut perpendicular to its inclination; E = the cornice profile with the epaulement. | FACTORY: From about the beginning of the XV c. the newel stops being made of one block per step and becomes ONE piece with mortises cut up the rake — Viollet says the same change happened in stone at the same date. The Montaigu newel came from a single timber 12 to 15 m tall. Generator: one lathe/screw primitive + a helical array of mortise cuts + two helical rib sweeps + a helical handrail sweep, all sharing one pitch.

subject: fig.32 — the PIVOTING wooden vis (escalier pivotant), after Mathurin Jousse
note: fig. 32 | DRAWING: coupe B (upper) + plan A (lower) | SEEN: Section: a masonry cylinder, the timber stair inside quite independent of it; the arbre/noyau O runs the full height as a single shaft; at the foot the iron pivot G with I above it; the first steps and then, higher, the steps relieved by short liens K; landings framed into the masonry at two levels at the right; a cylindrical timber partition with door openings. Plan: hatched masonry cylinder with landings/openings at A (left) and D (lower left), the timber cylinder inside, the newel hatched at the centre with radial treads (solid in the upper half, dashed in the lower), E and F on the horizontal, H just below F, C the first step at the lower left. | FACTORY: Type PIVOTING_VIS — a defensive device, for logis 'ou l'on avait a craindre les surprises de nuit', in manoirs and donjons. Mechanism: steps E to F are FIXED and independent of the rotating newel; from step H upward everything (steps, spiral limon, cylindrical timber partition pierced with doors) bears on the pivoting arbre O, which turns on an iron pivot below and is held at the top in a ring formed in two horizontal timbers; the first four steps off H are relieved by long potences I, the rest by shorter liens K to keep headroom. A quarter turn of the cylinder masks every door on every floor; the gap between F and H stops an intruder, and a simple arret placed on a landing locks the whole thing. Viollet believes the invention is very old and reports finding cylindrical masonry cages with doors at each level and NO trace of any stone or timber stair — inference, not proof.

subject: House carved on a capital of the primitive church of Vezelay, earlier than the early-12th-c rebuilding; Viollet cites it as evidence of timber building
note: fig. 1 | DRAWING: sculpture copy | FACTORY: Viollet's own footnote says this is a house sculpted on a capital, i.e. a conventionalised image, not a measured building. Treat as weak evidence.

subject: House copied from a capital of the cloister of Moissac (12th c); shows an external stair
note: fig. 2 | DRAWING: sculpture copy | FACTORY: Cited by Viollet for the escalier exterieur / grand perron, which he says plays an important role in 11th-12th-c houses.

subject: Composite type-plan and street facade of a house of the beginning of the 12th c
note: fig. 3 | DRAWING: plan + elevation | SEEN: Plan (street at bottom): front salle A occupying the full width; passage/degagement B down the left rear with a spiral stair (limacon) drawn as a circle in the rear-left corner; back room C (kitchen) lit from the court D beyond the rear wall; the whole is two rooms deep (batiment double). Elevation: ashlar ground storey with a two-light round-headed window; an external stair (perron) curving up to a closed landing carried on corbelling and an angle colonnette, with the cellar descent sheltered beneath it; the whole first storey is a jettied pan de bois whose window band occupies well over half the frontage; heavily projecting eaves roof with tile cresting. Scaled off the 5 m bar: about 8.5 m wide x 11 m deep externally (+/-10%). | FACTORY: This is the master generator template for the French 12th-c town house: stone base + timber jettied upper + rear court. Parts: perron with bench landing, closed second landing on corbel/colonnette, cellar hatch under the landing, peephole beside the door, spiral stair at rear-left, court with shared well. Viollet's footnote says the plan is a COMPOSITE from plans collected in Burgundy, the Nivernais and haute Champagne - so it is a type, not a single building: perfect for a parametric generator, useless as a citation for one house. | VERIFICATION: bar x=464->553 = 89 px for 5 m = 17.8 px/m; walls x=221->390 = 169 px = 9.5 m wide; depth y=42->238 = 196 px = 11.0 m. The reader's 8.5 m width is 11 per cent low and outside its own stated +/-10 per cent band; the 11 m depth is exact. NOTE the method claim 'the engraved bars run about 59 to 62 pixels per metre' is FALSE AS WRITTEN - 59-62 px is one bar DIVISION, and the division is 1 m on figs 12/14/15/16 but 10 m on fig 17 and about 17.3-17.8 px/m here. Read each bar's LABEL before scaling.

subject: House of the town of Cluny, 12th c: ground-floor and first-floor plans
note: fig. 4 | DRAWING: plan (2 levels) | SEEN: Both plans have the street at the bottom. Ground floor A: allee with straight stair (degre droit) C along the left party wall; boutique D filling the street frontage; open galerie/portique E along the left of an open court F drawn with a diagonal cross; well G; kitchen H at the far rear with its great chimney I in the back wall. First floor B: stair arrival K, salle L over the shop, glazed or open galerie N along the court with a small stair up to the galetas, chamber O over the kitchen. Scaled off the 10 m bar: plot roughly 8 m wide x 20 m deep (+/-10%). | FACTORY: The canonical deep burgage plot: shop-front block, open court with a covered gallery on one side, detached kitchen block at the rear, all on a plot 8 x 20 m. Generator sequence: front block (2 storeys + galetas) -> court -> gallery strip -> kitchen block; stair against one party wall, court well on the shared boundary. | VERIFICATION: the bar is 10 equal divisions x=29->202 with a taller mid-tick and the label '10' = 17.3 px/m. External walls x=69->181 = 112 px = 6.5 m (7.0 m if the flanking outline lines are counted); depth y=37->356 = 319 px = 18.4 m. So the canonical deep burgage plot is about 6.5 x 18.5 m, NOT 8 x 20 m - which also removes the reader's internal contradiction with its own fig-5 frontage of 6.9 m.

subject: The same Cluny house: general section on ab (A), street elevation (B), and vertical profile with the surviving level C
note: fig. 5 | DRAWING: section + elevation | SEEN: Section A cuts through front block, court and rear block: ground storey masonry, timber upper with an open gallery to the court, tall chimney stack. Elevation B: ashlar ground storey pierced by one large round-headed shop arch (goods on a counter, a figure standing in it) and a narrower grilled door for the allee; first storey an unbroken arcature of seven round-headed windows on shafts over a corbel-table string; above it an open timber loggia (the galetas) under a wide projecting tiled roof. Scaled off the 5 m bar: facade about 6.9 m wide, ground storey about 4 m high, eaves about 9 m (+/-10%). | FACTORY: CONJECTURE FLAG: the text says the facade survives only up to level C and that only the galetas storey has been destroyed - so the top timber loggia storey as drawn is Viollet's restitution. Model it as an optional top storey. The seven-bay arcature over a 6.9 m front gives a window module of about 0.95 m.

subject: Double (twin) house at Montreal, Yonne, first years of the 13th c: ground-floor plan
note: fig. 6 | DRAWING: plan | SEEN: Street at the bottom. Two mirrored dwellings C and C' either side of one central party wall running front to back. A = the two entrances with perrons and stone benches; B = the two cellar descents opening directly on the public way (stated to be the Burgundian habit); D = two small rear courts ringed with single-storey timber lean-tos (appentis); the stair cage is shared in the middle at the rear with separate flights, landing E serving C and F serving C', with upper doors G and H; I = one well shared between the two houses, on the rear wall axis. Dark strips at the far left and right are the neighbours across the lateral ruelles. Scaled off the 10 m bar: about 12.9 m overall x 12.7 m deep, i.e. about 6.4 m per dwelling (+/-10%). | FACTORY: A ready-made town-generator primitive: the semi-detached pair. Two plots merged to recover the land of one alley; one common party wall, one common stair cage with split flights, one common well, one roof. 6.4 m per dwelling is the plot-width datum. | VERIFICATION: bar = 29.2 px/m. Overall x=85->430 = 11.8 m wide, y=29->400 = 12.7 m deep, i.e. about 5.9 m external per dwelling (5.3 m internal) - not 12.9 m / 6.4 m per dwelling. The 6.4 m 'plot-width datum' should be 5.9 m.

subject: The same Montreal double house: street facade
note: fig. 7 | DRAWING: elevation (perspective) | SEEN: Gable to the street, shared between the two dwellings (pignon commun). A central pilaster/buttress rises through the gable to a finial carrying a carved figure; two front buttresses with corbelling carry a continuous first-floor balcony with a stone arcaded balustrade of colonnettes; below, the two doors with stone bench and perron steps, and the cellar descents; behind the balcony, two-light and paired arched windows. The roof verge oversails the facade very deeply so that both perrons, both cellar descents and both balconies are covered. | FACTORY: Verifies the stated rule 'la saillie du toit a deux egouts avec pignon commun, de sorte que les deux perrons, les deux descentes de caves et les deux balcons sont abrites'. Generator: deep gable-end verge overhang as the weather strategy, not a jetty.

subject: House on the square of Saint-Antonin (Tarn-et-Garonne), mid-13th c
note: fig. 8 | DRAWING: elevation | SEEN: Four levels. Ground: three tall pointed arcades used as market stalls with cloth curtains hung under the arches. First and second floors: continuous arcatures, each bay of four pointed lights divided by narrow trumeaux, with pierced roundels in the spandrels. Iron ring-hooks are visible on the window jambs at springing level on both upper floors. Top: the galetas as an open timber loggia under a projecting tile roof with round-tile cresting. Scaled off the 5 m bar: about 9.9 m frontage; ground arcade about 4.6 m high; upper storeys about 3.7 and 4.0 m; eaves about 14 m (+/-10%). | FACTORY: The Midi 'monumental' town house. Note the ground arcade is a market device (curtains under the arches on market days), not a portico. Iron ring-hooks are a repeatable facade fitting keyed to the window module. | VERIFICATION REFUTES 'each bay of four pointed lights divided by narrow trumeaux' and 'four lights per window bay'. The French is 'Les grandes salles du premier et du second etage sont eclairees largement par des arcatures continues, qui a l'interieur forment quatre fenetres separees par des trumeaux etroits' = the continuous arcatures form FOUR WINDOWS AS SEEN FROM INSIDE. The plate shows EIGHT arcature lights per storey, paired under roundels. The reader's own vocabulary entry had this right and its figure entry contradicted it.

subject: The bannes (fabric awnings) of the Saint-Antonin type of house: assembly details
note: fig. 9 | DRAWING: detail + section | SEEN: A = the anneau-crochet (ring-and-hook) sealed into the masonry with the pole passing through the ring; D = the tie hooks; B = the socketed scarf by which one perche is emmanchee into the next, so the poles run in bay-length modules. Main drawing: the cloth slung from the horizontal pole across a window bay, gathered, with a deep frilled valance hanging at the front; prop-poles C lift the outer edge and cords crossing beneath in croix de saint Andre hold the fall and are tied back to hooks D. The right-hand drawing labelled Coupe is the section showing the prop-pole angle from sill to awning edge. | FACTORY: Fully parametric street-dressing kit: ring spacing = window bay; pole = bay-length module with socket joints; two prop-poles per bay; crossed under-cords; weighted frilled valance whose stated function is both shade and to keep the prop-poles inclined. Cheap, high-value town-set detail.

subject: House in the rue Saint-Martin, Amiens, 1230-40; compared to Beauvais and Soissons of the same date
note: fig. 9bis | DRAWING: elevation | SEEN: All-stone facade, gable to the street with a lancet in the gable. Ground floor: a wide segmental-arched porte cochere, a small pedestrian door, and a broad shop window with iron grille and traceried head. First and second floors: each an unbroken arcature of four bays of two-light windows on colonnettes under relieving arches, with string courses at floor level. Chimney stack at the right on the party wall. Scaled off the 5 m bar: about 9.3 m frontage; ground storey about 4.8 m; upper storeys about 3.7 and 4.1 m; gable apex about 16 m (+/-10%). | FACTORY: CONJECTURE FLAG: Viollet states 'Nous avons retabli le pignon et le rez-de-chaussee d'apres d'autres fragments du meme temps et des memes contrees' - only the two arcatured upper storeys are surviving fabric. Use the arcatures as evidence, the gable and shopfront as reconstruction.

subject: House at Caussade (Tarn-et-Garonne), mid-13th c, brick
note: fig. 10 | DRAWING: elevation + side profile | SEEN: Facade almost entirely brick; hard Caylus stone confined to the pier bases, window colonnettes, bandeaux and sommiers, exactly as the text states. Four storeys: ground with two large pointed brick arcades containing shop counters and wares; first and second floors with pairs of twin windows under big brick relieving arches; third floor with smaller paired windows; then a timber band with croix de Saint-Andre under a widely projecting eaves. Iron ring-hooks for the bannes on the window jambs. Scaled off the 5 m bar: about 8.4 m frontage; storeys about 4.7, 4.2, 3.9 m plus a 1.9 m timber loft; eaves about 14.7 m (+/-10%). | FACTORY: Material-substitution variant of the Saint-Antonin type: same massing, brick shell with stone only at load points and mouldings. Gives a clean rule for a brick-town material set: stone = bases, colonnettes, string courses, springers; brick = everything else.

subject: One bay of the facade of the Maison des Musiciens, rue du Tambour, Reims, about 1240-50
note: fig. 11 | DRAWING: elevation of one bay | FACTORY: Useful as the 'rich north-French merchant/guild house': simple construction, rich ornament, sculpture in the trumeaux between wide windows. Possibly the house of the confrerie of ministrels.

subject: Burgundian house type with the spiral stair planted in the street wall: ground-floor plan (Avallon, Flavigny, Semur-en-Auxois, Dijon)
note: fig. 12 | DRAWING: plan | SEEN: Street at the bottom. The vis A sits in the middle of the street facade and bulges out as a half-round projection, partly corbelled over the entrance door B; door C, placed left or right according to the way the stair gironne, opens into the first room D, from which one passes into E and then F, the same at every storey; door G at the rear leads from the middle room E to a court or small garden. Scaled off the 5 m bar: about 9.9 m frontage x 6.1 m deep, three rooms in file parallel to the street (+/-10%). | FACTORY: The second French urban type, and the opposite of the burgage plot: broad-fronted, one room deep, rooms in file, stair in the FRONT wall doubling as ground-floor vestibule. Stated reason it is regional: Burgundy has excellent hard stone able to carry a thin turret corbelled on the tread-ends of the first revolution. Generator: enfilade of 3 rooms, stair-turret at facade centre, door beside it on the side determined by the stair's hand. | VERIFICATION: scales to 9.73 x 5.88 m against the reader's 9.9 x 6.1 - confirmed. Broad-front Burgundian type, the inverse proportion to the burgage plot.

subject: The same Burgundian type: street elevation
note: fig. 13 | DRAWING: elevation | SEEN: The round stair turret stands in the middle of the facade, corbelled forward on the stepped soffit of the treads, rises through two storeys and is capped by a conical shingled spire with a figure finial. Door B at its foot, sheltered by the projection. Cellar entrance O, a segmental opening under the sill (allege) of a ground-floor window at the right. Ground floor: two-light trefoiled windows; upper floor: paired lights with colonnettes under arcades. At the eaves a stone chene0u carried on projecting corbels, sloping to a gargoyle at the end. Steep roof laid in patterned polychrome tiles in lozenges, with ridge cresting. | FACTORY: Verifies two Burgundian signatures at once: the facade stair turret and the stone eaves gutter with end gargoyles on corbels. Patterned lozenge tiling is a cheap high-impact regional texture rule for a Burgundian town.

subject: House at Vitteaux (Cote-d'Or), second half of the 13th c: ground-floor plan
note: fig. 14 | DRAWING: plan | SEEN: Street at the bottom. The stair cage projects at the right end of the street front: A the entrance door beneath it, B the cellar door opening on the street. Through the door is a small vestibule C, straight ahead the kitchen D, to the left the salle (lettered E on the plate). The rear wall on the garden side is drawn as a pan de bois, matching the text. Scaled off the 5 m bar: about 7.5 x 6.9 m, i.e. roughly 52 sq m footprint - a good cross-check on the stated 49 sq m of building (+/-10%). | FACTORY: The costed reference house. Only the front wall and the two party walls are masonry; the floors bear on the two party walls and on the middle pan de bois. The same distribution repeats on the first floor giving two chambers, and the second floor under the roof is one large room split in the depth of the building. Cheapest possible generator variant: 3 masonry walls + 1 timber spine + 1 timber rear wall. | VERIFICATION: the cross-check is genuine - scaled 7.55 x 6.79 = 51.3 sq m against the stated 49 'metres superficiels'. But note the reader's own caveat: the text says the floors bear 'sur le pan de bois du milieu' while the plan draws that wall like masonry; do not treat the timber middle spine as certain.

subject: The same Vitteaux house: street elevation
note: fig. 15 | DRAWING: elevation | SEEN: Three storeys of stone, the top one in the gable. Stair turret at the right, no longer corbelled on the tread-ends but on a well-cut raking flat course (plate-bande rampante), visible as the sweeping curved corbel; at its top the cylinder becomes hexagonal to make the shingle roof easier to lay. Door A with ironwork at the turret foot; cellar door B with segmental head to the right. A ferme boiteuse projects over the whole facade, sprung from the stair projection and from a corbel plumb with the left jambe-etriere; a wooden gargoyle throws the gutter water left onto the street. Two chimney stacks on the party walls at the left, their heads visible. Windows: 3 lights at ground level, 4 at the first floor, 3 in the gable. Scaled off the 5 m bar: storeys about 3.4 and 3.3 m, ridge about 13 m over a 7.5-8.5 m front (+/-10%). | FACTORY: The clearest single lesson in the article for a generator: a half-truss (ferme boiteuse) can be hung off two existing projections - the stair turret and one corbel - to shelter a whole facade for almost nothing. Also the cylinder-to-hexagon transition at the turret head, whose stated reason is to simplify the shingle covering. | VERIFICATION: storeys re-measured at 3.25 m and 3.36 m (reader 3.4 / 3.3), ridge 13.0 m (reader 13). Confirmed. Remember the article states NO storey height anywhere - every storey height is inferred from a plate.

subject: House in the rue de Paris, Provins, second half of the 13th c
note: fig. 16 | DRAWING: elevation | SEEN: Gable to the street. Ground floor a nearly blank rubble (moellon) wall with quoins, pierced only by one window and one door with elaborate ironwork - the inhabitant shuts himself in. First floor, the salle: two wide two-light transomed windows under large stone relieving arches. Two more small windows in the gable. Carved corbels/gargoyles at the springing level of the eaves. Scaled off the 5 m bar: about 9.3 m frontage; ground storey about 5.5 m, confirming the stated 'etages hauts entre planchers'; apex about 16 m (+/-10%). | FACTORY: The closed variant. Rule stated with a reason: relieving arches in stone carry the wall over the window voids so that a plain rubble wall with big openings still stands. Use as the type for a landowner/rentier town (Provins, Laon) as against a manufacturing town (Reims, Troyes, Beauvais, Amiens). | VERIFICATION REFUTES the reader's window count. The reader recorded 'two wide two-light transomed windows under large stone relieving arches' on the first floor. Cropped and enlarged, the plate shows FOUR two-light transomed windows, each under its own pointed head, GROUPED IN TWO PAIRS under two relieving arches. Scaled dimensions stand: ground storey 5.43 m (reader 5.5), frontage 9.33 m (9.3), apex 15.6 m (16).

subject: One block (ilot) of houses of the bastide of Montpazier, founded about 1284
note: fig. 17 | DRAWING: plan | SEEN: Five identical cells in a row. Each has a straight stair against one lateral wall about halfway back, a fireplace on a lateral wall, and a partition dividing a front and a back room. Between neighbouring cells there is not one party wall but TWO independent walls with a hairline gap - the endronne or gutter-width alley, exactly as Viollet's footnote states for Montpazier. The block is flanked by wider gaps to the neighbouring blocks: about 7.5 m on one side and about 3.5 m on the other, matching the stated 10 m street and 3 m rear ruelle. Scaled off the 10/20/30 m bar: each house about 7.6 m frontage x about 21.6 m deep (+/-10%). | FACTORY: The single most valuable plate in the article for a town generator: a repeatable, identical, uniformly lotted cell with an exact plot ratio (about 7.6 x 21.6 m, i.e. roughly 1:3), no party walls, a hairline drainage alley between each pair, two streets of unequal width, and one stair + one hearth per cell. Instantiate by array. | VERIFICATION (PNG decoded): the plate's own bar has ticks at x=108.5/168.0/227.5/287.0 labelled 10/20/30, i.e. 59.5 px per TEN-metre division = 5.95 px/m. Street gap (block face x=167.5 to facing block x=107.5) = 60-64 px = 10.1-10.8 m, CONFIRMING Viollet's stated 'une rue de 10 metres de largeur'; rear gap x=289->308 = 19 px = 3.2 m, confirming 'une ruelle de 3 metres environ'. The reader's claimed 7.5 m plate figure and its 25 per cent text/plate discrepancy DO NOT EXIST. Corrected cell: 8.3 m frontage (pitch 49.6 px) x 20.2 m deep (120 px), plot ratio ~1:2.4, not 7.6 x 21.6 / 1:3. The endronne between cells is a 0.4-0.8 m slot between two independent walls.

subject: Plan of a quarter of the square of the bastide of Montpazier
note: fig. 18 | DRAWING: plan | SEEN: The corner of the square with its surrounding portiques drawn as arcades on square piers, the arcade bays dashed in. Each house corresponds to one arcade bay of about 7.7 m. The corner houses have pans coupes - the angle cut back diagonally - and the streets debouch at the corners, not at the middles of the sides. A marks the viewpoint of fig 19.
