Scaled off the 10/20 m bar: portico depth about 3.5 m (+/-10%). | FACTORY: Encodes the stated town-planning rule: never pierce a street through the middle of a side of the square, because people crossing would obstruct people gathering; put circulation on the sides and leave the centre out of traffic; chamfer the angle houses so carts can turn in diagonally on market days.

subject: Perspective of one of the entrances to the square of Montpazier, taken from point A of fig 18
note: fig. 19 | DRAWING: perspective view | SEEN: Wide, low arcades (couverts) on massive piers, with segmental and pointed heads. At the chamfered corner the upper storey is carried out on corbelling over the pan coupe. Upper walls with plain windows and a corbelled cornice/eaves course; low-pitched Midi roofs. | FACTORY: Gives the three-dimensional consequence of fig 18: jettied corner over the chamfer. A town-corner asset: pier arcade + pan coupe + corbelled angle above.

subject: House at Chateaudun drawn by Viollet in 1841, beginning of the 14th c: plan and elevation
note: fig. 20 | DRAWING: plan + elevation | SEEN: Plan (street at bottom, lettered A): a large shop filling the frontage with a central post (visible as a small black square) and a stub of cross-wall B; a pierced spiral stair; corridor C leading to court D and back room E. A dimension line lettered on the plan gives the depth as 16 m. Scaling that, the frontage is about 7.7 m. Elevation: ground and first storeys in stone with rubble party walls; two segmental shop openings with shutter hooks; at the first floor two wide three-light traceried openings set under two flat relieving arches, the openings themselves being very pierced stone frames (chassis en pierre); above, the timber gable with a truss standing forward of the wall face, its ends carried on the sablieres eased by curved liens and its ridge purlin (filiere d'axe) also eased by a lien; big arched brace in the gable, finial at the apex; chimney stack at the left; G and H mark the two joist levels. Storeys about 3.2 and 3.4 m, apex about 12.6 m. | FACTORY: The transitional stage: masonry house with a projecting timber roof truss but NO jetty (the text notes the comble storey here is not corbelled). Model the projecting gable truss as a separate component that can be added to a masonry shell. Also records that at first-floor level the main beam passes THROUGH the front wall and receives the roof tie-beams (entraits), which is why the truss can stand forward. | VERIFICATION REFUTES the reader's window count: not 'two wide three-light traceried openings under two flat relieving arches' but FOUR two-light traceried stone frames, two under each relieving arch - eight lights, none of three. The plate-lettered depth of 16 m IS right (independently corroborated at 16.3 m from the elevation's own 5 m bar, x=179->476 = 297 px giving a 7.86 m frontage on a 239x115 px plan).

subject: House at Laval on a steeply sloping street, somewhat later than fig 20: plan and elevation
note: fig. 21 | DRAWING: plan + elevation | SEEN: One building divided for two households by a pan de bois de refend on the axis of the facade, from top to bottom; plan P shows each household with its own stair from shop to first floor. The street slope lets the left household have an entresol A (joist levels B and C) while the right has only a raised ground floor and a first floor (joist level C'). The first-floor pan de bois stands forward of the ground-floor frame on three corbelled sablieres, and is itself sheltered by the ferme de tete of the roof set on the ends of the sablieres S. Visible: stone plinth stepping down with the street, shop counters with hanging cloths, curved liens under the sabliere ends, croix de Saint-Andre in the window alleges, a tall traceried gable with a big arched brace, a chimney on the right party wall. Scaled off the 5 m bar: about 8.6 m for the two dwellings, i.e. about 4.3 m each; apex about 15.4 m (+/-10%). | FACTORY: KEY STRUCTURAL STATEMENT, verified by the drawing: 'Les poteaux corniers de face ne sont la que pour maintenir le pan de bois sur la rue, car derriere ces poteaux corniers s'elevent les murs mitoyens en moellon portant cheminees.' The timber front is NOT the structure - the rubble party walls are, and they carry the chimneys. Also the slope-driven entresol: use street gradient as a generator input that produces a half-storey.

subject: House at Annonay (Ardeche), classed by Viollet as 14th c
note: fig. 22 | DRAWING: perspective view | SEEN: Ground floor of large stone blocks. On it a thick fir enrayure whose third course forms the floor and oversails to carry, in corbelling, the first-floor pan de bois, whose front face is made of three superposed jointed sablieres onto which the montants are assembled; two corner posts hold the ends of the three sablieres; laterally, ordinary pans de bois hourdes in rubble and mortar form the party walls (big X-braces visible on the flank). A second cantilever floor (plancher en bascule) carries a second pan de bois storey, the whole crowned by a roof projecting very far over the street on long raking outriggers. | FACTORY: Verifies the stated 3.50 m roof projection beyond the ground-floor wall face, with the reason given twice: to keep rain and snow off the facade in a climate hot in summer and very harsh in winter, AND to shelter the steep streets so people can circulate in winter. A generator rule where roof overhang is a function of climate and street gradient, not of style.

subject: House at Nantua (Ain), roughly contemporary with the Annonay house, closer to the Swiss chalet
note: fig. 23 | DRAWING: perspective view | SEEN: Masonry ground floor of large blocks. The projecting first-floor front is built of horizontally stacked timbers (empilage) - clearly different from a studded frame - while the return flank is an assembled pan de bois with X-braces of the north-French kind. Doubled sablieres under the roof. The front truss (ferme de face) projects to form an auvent. Wrought-iron sign bracket; wide overhanging shingled roof. | FACTORY: The hybrid: log-stacked front, assembled frame flank. Exactly what the text claims - primitive empilage traditions mixed with assembled carpentry from the north. Good evidence that the two timber systems coexist in one building, so a generator can mix them per wall rather than per building.

subject: House at Perpignan, later converted to the palais de justice; facade of almost antique taste with Aragonese detail
note: fig. 24 | DRAWING: elevation | FACTORY: Evidence for the dating trap: in provinces that were not French in the 14th c (Roussillon), Romanesque forms persist. A generator must decouple style-age from build-date by region.

subject: House at Trier (Treves), beginning of the 14th c, showing its chimney in the middle of the street gable
note: fig. 25 | DRAWING: elevation + hearth plan + chimney cap | SEEN: Stone facade with a stepped (corbie) gable to the street. The flue rises in the middle of the gable wall, carried out on corbelling from the first floor on three consoles shaped like capitals and on two small arches set between the first-floor windows; it continues up the gable to the crowning cap B, drawn separately as a cylindrical shaft with a hood. A is the fragment of plan showing the hearth against the front wall. A carved lion sits on a set-back of the gable; the ground floor has a pointed door with ironwork and small windows; the first floor two tall two-light trefoiled windows. Scaled off the 5 m bar: about 9 m frontage, ground storey about 4.5 m, gable about 15 m (+/-10%). | FACTORY: A dating rule with a stated reason: hearth against the STREET wall with the flue corbelled out under the facade from the first floor up is, in France, a 12th- or early-13th-c disposition; it survives to the 14th c on the Rhine. Viollet's stated rationale is comfort - you warm yourself and see out, and windows either side of the flue let you work by the fire without the glare of the flame.

subject: House at Beauvais, beginning of the 15th c (still standing on the square in 1834)
note: fig. 26 | DRAWING: elevation | SEEN: Eaves to the street (mur goutterot) with a big roof overhang and a crested ridge; two dormers in the slope, one small and pointed, one large gabled lucarne with finials and figures. First floor a timber frame with two large traceried windows and X-braced panels. Ground floor a portico on posts with arched brackets, the shops set back behind it, the allee A at the left. Stone party wall and chimney at the right. Scaled off the 5 m bar: about 7.8 m frontage; portico about 3.3 m high; first floor about 4.3 m; eaves about 14.3 m (+/-10%). | FACTORY: The eaves-on variant, which the text says occurs when the plot is 'en bordure' (broader than deep): then the gables sit on the party walls and the street front is goutterot. Two rooms at the first floor reached by a spiral stair at the back of the allee A; one big room under the roof lit by two lucarnes, one to the street and one to a small court.

subject: House at Reims, Place des Marches, 15th c: timber facade preserved top to bottom, corbelled 1.65 m over the public way on five potences
note: fig. 26bis | DRAWING: perspective view | SEEN: The jetty is carried on heavy curved brackets sweeping out below the first floor, projecting the whole timber front over the shop front. Verified against the text: there is NO croix de Saint-Andre anywhere in the height of the frame, only posts, transoms and moulded panels, yet the carpentry is undeformed. At the right the stone party wall A carries the chimneys and its jambe-etriere receives two liens (the two carved brackets at the bottom right); on the other side the mitoyennete is only a simple pan de bois. The front takes a lateral light on the return face, which is why Viollet calls it a bretche. Numerous small leaded windows; carved figures on the intermediate posts (the applied statues on the corner post are lost; the two outer lower liens carry Samson killing the lion and Saint Michael overcoming the demon in half-relief). Panels hourdes in masonry and rendered. | FACTORY: The one measured jetty in the article: 1.65 m on five potences. Also the asymmetry rule - one flank a masonry party wall carrying flues, the other flank only a timber partition. And a counter-example to the bracing rule: a first-class frame can omit St-Andrew crosses if the joints are perfect.

subject: House at Rouen forming the angle of two streets, first half of the 15th c, four storeys of pan de bois
note: fig. 27 | DRAWING: elevation + section | SEEN: The section A at the left shows four successive corbelled steps, one per storey, so that the third floor occupies a sensibly greater area than the ground floor. The cornice at the base of the gable is a run of imitation machicolations. Windows numerous and small; the alleges beneath them filled with croix de Saint-Andre; at every storey long diagonal decharges carry the weight of the frame back to the corner posts; carved statuettes on the posts; shopfront with grilles and a pointed door. Scaled off the 5 m bar: about 7.5 m frontage; storeys about 3.1-3.4 m each; ridge about 16 m (+/-10%). | FACTORY: The cumulative-jetty geometry, in section: this is the plate to copy for a narrow-street generator, since it defines how much the street closes at each level. Note that both bracing devices - crosses in the alleges, decharges to the corner posts - are given explicit structural jobs (stop the jamb-posts leaning out; carry the storey weight to the corner posts).

subject: Another Rouen house, rue Malpalu, end of the 15th c: the timber facade become a lantern
note: fig. 28 | DRAWING: elevation | FACTORY: The end state of the timber-facade progression: maximum glazing, minimum solid, bracing confined to the aprons.

subject: Part of a dwelling of the abbey of Saint-Amand, Rouen: masonry ground floor with two storeys of pan de bois entirely faced in carved joinery panels
note: fig. 29 | DRAWING: elevation | FACTORY: The final substitution: hourdis hidden behind panelling. For a generator, this is a skin swap on the same frame.

subject: Part of one of two houses in the rue de la Grosse-Horloge, Rouen: timber house with Renaissance pilasters and bandeaux
note: fig. 30 | DRAWING: elevation | FACTORY: Dating rule: classical mouldings on a timber frame = 16th c, and Viollet flags them as constructionally false. A style layer that can be applied over the same frame geometry.

subject: One of the oldest surviving hotels, at Provins, belonging to a rich canon of Saint-Quiriace
note: fig. 31 | DRAWING: plan | FACTORY: The earliest hotel pattern: two blocks + vaulted through-passage, hall at first floor reached by an external timber stair, barrel-boarded roof. Note the hall is still at the FIRST floor, not the ground.

subject: Hotel in the grande rue of Cordes, first years of the 14th c: mixed hotel and shop-house
note: fig. 32 | DRAWING: plan | SEEN: Street at the bottom. Entry A between two shops L L that have no access to the court - probably let, or used by the owner. Main court B; small service court C reached by passage D; open room E, probably the stable; cellar F; a broad spiral stair G in a projecting polygonal cage giving into the great ground-floor hall H, raised seven steps above the court; passage I to a garden K lying outside the old rampart, against which the hotel backs (the rampart is the heavy black wall across the plan); terrace N with perron on the court facing the hall; recent buildings encroach on the garden from a to b. Scaled off the 10 m bar: site about 37 m wide x 34 m deep, plus about 15 m of garden beyond the rampart (+/-10%). | FACTORY: The southern merchant compromise: hotel behind, lettable shops on the street. Generator: street range of shops + entry passage -> court -> hall block raised on steps -> service court -> garden beyond the wall. Also records that the great hall can be at ground level in the Midi, reached up seven steps.

subject: Hotel of Jacques Coeur, Bourges, built from 1443: ground-floor plan
note: fig. 33 | DRAWING: plan | SEEN: The street runs down the right side. Entrance A, a porte cochere with poterne B beside it; stair F up to the chapel over the entrance so that the chapel can be reached without entering the house; great court C; closed portico D (used as the waiting place for the poor who were given the leftovers of the table, so that they never entered the hotel); portico E open onto a small court G with a shared well G'; principal stair H; great ground-floor dining hall I with an immense chimney c and a minstrels' tribune I' reached by its own stair f; a trap i in the floor of I down to the cellars; service gallery J to kitchens K and K', K' having an oven with chimney and a fourneau potager; a service corridor L and small court L' connecting the street directly to the kitchens, and L'' to the great court; office M with a serving turntable m; a vaulted and paved scullery under the oven with a gargoyle to a soakaway, and servants' latrines beside it under the stair mass; rooms T and T' with a wardrobe in the square tower R, forming with tower Q a complete independent apartment; concierge V; passage under stair O to the place de Berri P. Towers S, R, Q are old city rampart towers reused, and the open angle of the rampart on which the front wall was built forces the whole oblique geometry. Scaled off the 10/20 m bar: site about 35 x 55 m; the great dining hall about 11 x 12 m; the black chimney mark c measures about 5.7 m, corroborating the stated 6 m opening (+/-10%). | FACTORY: The best service-adjacency graph in the article. Explicit design rules: every service in its place, communications easy but independent, all symmetry sacrificed, every room big or small lit, numerous concealed degagements, and a separate street door for the kitchens. Also a site rule: build on a fief of the ramparts and reuse the towers, and the rampart alignment dictates the plan angles.

subject: Hotel of Jacques Coeur: first-floor plan
note: fig. 34 | DRAWING: plan | FACTORY: Eight named stairs on one floor: the generator lesson is that independence of services in a French hotel is bought with stairs, not with corridors. The dais in the great hall is the one clear parallel with the English hall.

subject: Hotel of Jacques Coeur: cavalier (bird's-eye) view taken from point P' of fig 33
note: fig. 35 | DRAWING: perspective view | FACTORY: Programmatic sculpture: the carving over each door advertises the function behind it. A cheap, very legible way to signpost rooms in a game building.

subject: Hotel de La Tremoille, rue des Bourdonnais, Paris, rebuilt about 1490, demolished 1840: ground-floor plan and general view X
note: fig. 36 | DRAWING: plan | FACTORY: A complete Parisian hotel adjacency list, including a stated storey-count rule: main logis 3 levels + cellars, service ranges 1 level. Note the gallery lit generously to the court and almost blind to the street - a directional glazing rule.

subject: Hotel de La Tremoille: facade of the main logis between the turret and the stair
note: fig. 37 | DRAWING: elevation | FACTORY: Records the asymmetry of display: rich court facade, plain garden facade, near-blind street wall. Useful ruleset for how much detail to spend on which face.

subject: Hotel de Cluny, Paris, begun 1485 and carried on from 1490: ground-floor plan
note: fig. 38 | DRAWING: plan | SEEN: The rue des Mathurins-Saint-Jacques runs along the bottom right behind a crenellated boundary wall with the main door A and poterne A'; the wall carried a timber chemin de ronde on corbels, now destroyed and replaced by iron brackets. Concierge B; portico C giving into the ground-floor rooms H, also reached by the great stair F and a small door f; kitchen D with its perron and its own stair P having issues outside, into the kitchen floor and into hall H'; door g from the court straight into the kitchen; room I returning onto the garden with an angle stair R opening onto the garden, onto I and onto gallery L; K an open hall, a kind of covered preau under the chapel at the first floor; court E; the reused antique halls of the Thermes at M (probably the stables) and beyond O; gallery L formerly leading to latrines; a small stair S from I down into the preau K and up to the chapel. The great stair F ends in a platform reached by a small vis from the roof storey. The chapel has an absidiole corbelled out on the outer pier of the covered preau, and four rib vaults on one central column. | FACTORY: Stated levels: cellars, ground floor, first floor and a mansarded roof storey - the same as La Tremoille. Old floors of beams carrying joists still exposed, several original chimneys. The garden is stated as about 17 x 35 m, though scaling the drawn parterre gives roughly 15 x 27 m, so treat the drawn garden outline as indicative only.

subject: Hotel de Cluny: cavalier view taken from the entrance side
note: fig. 39 | DRAWING: perspective view | FACTORY: Second reference elevation for the Paris hotel type.

subject: Old peasant house of the Morvan
note: fig. 40 | DRAWING: perspective view | SEEN: A mass of piled granite blocks. A very low ground floor used as cellar, store, hen-house or pigsty, entered by a low arched opening; the door raised one or two metres above the ground and reached by an external stone stair with a landing engaged in the wall thickness; small openings; a heavy roof covered in thin stone plates (laves in local speech) clearly drawn as overlapping slabs; chimney on the gable slope; a single room with its chimney per house. | FACTORY: Rural generator with an explicit growth rule: 'Chaque maison ne contient qu'une piece avec sa cheminee ; si l'on veut deux pieces, ce sont deux maisons qui se joignent par les pignons.' Extension happens by cell addition gable to gable, never by subdivision. No ornament at all; timbers barely squared; floor of beaten earth washed with granitic sand and clay.

subject: Peasant house of the Nivernais / haute Bourgogne
note: fig. 41 | DRAWING: perspective view | FACTORY: A quality gradient for rural assets, keyed to region and to proximity to an abbey: same programme, better finish. The projecting joist-ends forming an auvent and framing into the rafters is a specific, modellable detail.

subject: Peasant houses in the village of Rougemont, between Montbard and Aisy, mostly early 13th c
note: fig. 42 | DRAWING: perspective view | FACTORY: Dating/quality rule with a stated cause: monastic patronage raises rural building quality and pushes it into masonry. Also gives a rural street form - gables to the road, doors all on the same side, from the equal division of boels.

subject: Weakened survival of the Norman timber tradition still to be seen in the countryside of the Eure
note: fig. 43 | DRAWING: perspective view | FACTORY: The one French case that matches the English open hall: single tall room, central hearth, timber smoke flue, no upper floor. Note it is RURAL Normandy, not urban France. Decorated ridge poincons plus a carved crest board is a strong silhouette asset.

subject: Peasant house of the Vosges, near Gerardmer and Retournemer: plan and view
note: fig. 43bis | DRAWING: plan + perspective | SEEN: Plan A at ground level: entrance hall B, from which one passes either into the great room C or into the back room D which holds the only stair up to the roof storey. It is in C, lit from both ends, that the whole household gathers for meals and the evening, and where food is prepared. Verified in the view: low broad log-built (empilage) walls on a stone plinth; the roof covered in thin slabs and weighted down with loose stones, with long poles laid over it; the log courses visible in the gable; the windows all in the gable frames; a masonry chimney through the roof. Scaled off the vertical 10 m bar: about 15 m long x 10 m deep. | FACTORY: Stated numbers: three rooms on the ground and four under the roof; a plinth of large sandstone blocks about 1.00 m high; the great chimney with jambs, fireback, hood and flue in masonry is, with the socles, the ONLY non-timber part; covering of tiles or schistose sandstone, loaded with stones. A pan de bois runs down the middle of the length carrying the tops of the rafters, and it and the two lateral frames oversail both gables in corbelling to form pronounced auvents; a joisted floor bears on those three parallel frames; light comes only through the gable frames. That is a complete, closed generator spec.

subject: Rural house of the plains of Toulouse / Ariege / Aude near Limoux, relatively old, i.e. 15th c
note: fig. 44 | DRAWING: perspective view | FACTORY: The Mediterranean rural type: shallow, wide, oriented, with an attached open lean-to. Orientation is stated as a design input, unlike the northern types.

subject: Fortified rural house known as the Maison du brigand at Le Cannet near Cannes, half-way up the slope about 4 km from the sea
note: fig. 45 | DRAWING: perspective view | FACTORY: Isolated defensible farmstead: vertical circulation by ladder and trap only, no ground-floor door, hopper machicolations. Viollet says these were more likely pirates' than farmers' houses. Similar ones survive in Corsica.

subject: Fortified rural house near Bordeaux, formerly surrounded by a water-filled ditch
note: fig. 46 | DRAWING: perspective view | FACTORY: Viollet suspects these date from the English domination in Guienne and compares Wenham Hall in Suffolk, a small brick house of the end of the 13th c on the same system: a parallelogram with a spiral stair in a corner turret, raised entrance, steps engaged in the wall. A direct Anglo-French comparison, and a ready tower-farm asset: one room per floor, chimney each, trap to cellar, corner vis.

subject: The 16th-century geometrical rule for the thickness of an abutment, shown for three arch forms (near-semicircular, moderately pointed, sharply pointed)
note: fig. 32 bis | DRAWING: Construction / geometric diagram | SEEN: Three stacked panels, identical construction each time. Springing line A-B; the arch curve is divided into three equal parts giving D (upper left) and C (upper right); a dashed circle arc is swung from centre B with radius = chord BC; the chord C-B is produced downward-right to meet that arc at E; a vertical through E gives the outer face G, a vertical through B the inner face H; the pier thickness is the horizontal distance GH. Measured off the plate the ratio thickness/span falls as the arch sharpens: roughly 0.23, 0.19, 0.175 of the span for panels 1, 2, 3. For a TRUE semicircle the construction closes exactly at thickness = R/2 = span/4 (E lands at x=1.5R, y=-0.866R), and the measured 0.23 for panel 1 is consistent with a slightly pointed drawn arch. | FACTORY: Directly implementable: buttress_depth = f(arch_form). Semicircle -> span/4. Two-centred -> less, scaling with sharpness. Note Viollet's own validity limit: only for piers of equal height not exceeding 1.5x the arch base.

subject: Roman semicircular barrel vault: pressure curve AB, thrust BC, wall height FD, required thickness CD, and the 'useless' triangle of masonry EDF
note: fig. 33 | DRAWING: Coupe (section) / thrust diagram | FACTORY: Gives the Gothic-vs-Roman wall-mass argument as a shape subtraction: the Roman wall contains a triangle of stone the thrust line never uses.

subject: Half-section of a three-aisled Gothic nave, with the plan diagram of thrust resolution inset at lower left
note: fig. 34 | DRAWING: Coupe (section) + plan diagram | SEEN: Lower left inset: three oblique thrusts BA, CA, DA meeting at A and resolving in plan into AE. In section: springing G, a freehand dotted thrust line G-H descending through the springer T, past the corbelled capital M at O and the capital at I, reaching the floor at H, clearly OUTBOARD of the axis P of the lower monocylindrical column. K = the flying buttress springing from the buttress head R. L = the aisle vault, its thrust bearing on column P. R-S = the superimposed vertical load. The corbelled capitals visibly step OUTWARD going up so their projection follows the direction GH. | FACTORY: Assembly rule: the pier is a stack of corbelled (en decharge) capitals whose successive offsets track a straight oblique line from vault springing to floor; the offset per storey is the parameter. Flag: the thrust line is drawn by eye, never computed.

subject: Plan slice of the apse and ambulatory of Notre-Dame-du-Port, Clermont: how a groin is obtained on a radial (trapezoidal) bay by stilting the narrower arch
note: fig. 36 | DRAWING: Detail plan | SEEN: The annular barrel CC' over the ambulatory; a wide half-cylinder A penetrating it over the outer opening HF, and a narrower one B over the inner opening EG. Their penetrations give the crossed plan lines EF and GH. Because the portico is on a circular plan, HF > EG; a semicircle on EG would crown far below the one on HF and would give no groin at all, only a small cylinder piercing a large one. The fix drawn here: the arch on EG is STILTED, shown by the rabattement IKM taking a rise NM equal to the rise OP of the wide arch, so both crowns M and P land on one horizontal line - which in turn fixes the rise of the annular barrel CC'. Four columns R, S, T, V with their tailloirs at one level. | FACTORY: Radial-bay generator rule: given two unequal spans that must crown level, stilt the narrower arch by (rise_wide - semicircular_rise_narrow) rather than changing its radius. Directly parameterisable.

subject: Springing of the ambulatory vaults on a monocylindrical column, choir of Langres cathedral: the wedge-shaped tailloir and the three superposed springers
note: fig. 37 | DRAWING: Perspective + plan inset | SEEN: Monocylindrical shaft with a quasi-Roman Corinthian capital. Plan inset X: the tailloir has two NON-PARALLEL sides forming a wedge (coin), so the intrados of the archivoltes A stays a true portion of a cylinder rather than a warped surface; on the ambulatory side the tailloir plan is a broken line to give a projecting seat to the arc doubleau B. Above the tailloir a corbelled projection C. THREE springers one above the other: the first two E and F have horizontal beds, the third G carries the cuts normal to the rib curves. The arc ogive D barely clears the mass and has to be embedded between the voussoirs of the archivoltes and doubleaux; the second arch I is thrown above the ogive, once the ogive has cleared the springers, to double the archivolte A because the wall over it is thick and carries a cul-de-four. Web courses in the ramping cells run roughly parallel to the wall arch. | FACTORY: Two hard rules: (1) wedge-shaped abacus keeps rib intrados cylindrical on radial plans, at the cost of an ugly capital that is sharper on the ambulatory side; (2) springer stack = N courses with horizontal beds then one with radial cuts. Both are cheap to parameterise.

subject: Section of the ramping ambulatory vault at Langres: the inclined ridge line, the roof slope A, the gallery B
note: fig. 39 | DRAWING: Coupe (section) | FACTORY: Ramping-vault generator: crown line is a straight incline between two unequal crowns; the roof slope and gallery floor are consequences, not independent choices.

subject: Method 1, USING the thrust: monolithic corbel stones tailed into the buttress, set on the thrust line itself, so the oblique load is drawn off along its own direction
note: fig. 40 | DRAWING: Coupe (section) / construction diagram | SEEN: Section with a human figure at lower left for scale (~1.7 m, making the drawn section roughly 13-14 m tall). The high vault springs at A on a bundle of en-delit shafts standing on pier X. A dotted straight thrust line runs from A down to B, leaving the line of the pier and passing INTO the buttress mass, reaching the ground at B well outboard of E, the axis of the lower shaft. Two large single stones C and D are corbelled out at exactly the level where that line crosses the pier, and are tailed (engagees a la queue) into the buttress behind, so the oblique load is delivered straight into the buttress instead of into the shaft below. Below them the pier continues as a slender shaft down to E, carrying no oblique load at all. Flying buttress G lands on the pier head. Buttress wall at the right with a water-spout. | FACTORY: A distinctive assembly pattern worth generating: a slender lower shaft that does NOT continue the load path, interrupted by two monolithic corbel stones that hand the thrust sideways into the buttress. Note Viollet's claim that this is STRONGER than a full pier under the springer - a bending-resistance claim about a single stone, which should be flagged rather than repeated.

subject: Method 2, the 'methode preventive': oppose thrust AB with a weaker opposite thrust CD and load the two springings with a weight E, converting both obliques into a vertical
note: fig. 40 bis | DRAWING: Construction diagram | FACTORY: Two-mode buttressing model for a generator: OPPOSE (flyer) vs PREVENT (asymmetric spans + superimposed dead load). Choose per storey.

subject: Plan of one apse bay of Notre-Dame de Chalons-sur-Marne at four levels: A ground, B vaulted first-floor gallery, C triforium, D vault springings
note: fig. 41 | DRAWING: Plan (4 levels) | FACTORY: Two reusable tricks: (1) insert extra columns to convert trapezoids into parallelograms; (2) polygonal inside / circular outside, so wall arcs are straight in plan while the envelope stays round.

subject: Perspective of the Chalons ambulatory with a chapel entrance; single isolated capital receiving all the ribs
note: fig. 42 | DRAWING: Perspective | FACTORY: Threshold rule: below a certain abacus area you must switch from side-by-side voussoirs to one interpenetrated springer stone.

subject: Section through the choir of Notre-Dame de Chalons-sur-Marne on line MN: aisle, vaulted gallery, triforium, clerestory, two tiers of flyers
note: fig. 43 | DRAWING: Coupe (section) + detail U | SEEN: Monocylindrical column A; aisle archivolte and vault springing B; RAMPING gallery vault G whose formeret C, being wider at the base than the archivolte D, crowns higher and so opens large windows; triforium E; roof F over the gallery. Monolithic shafts set EN DELIT (against the natural bed) around a coursed core - shaft H at aisle level, engaged column I at gallery level, column V standing on the outer triforium wall 'comme une forte chandelle de charpente'. Lower flyer L carrying the gallery vault thrust out to a remote abutment; upper flyer S springing not from the wall face M but ADVANCED to O, giving a deep abutment O-P; extra load R on the abutment; arch Q thrown under the springer T which acts as a lintel in the triforium. Pier X is corbelled OUT over the lower column Y. Detail U: the flyer voussoirs pass toward the arch centre above column V as if it did not exist, and a simple stone wedge (cale a) fills the angle between the abacus and the voussoirs. Scale bar at lower left: 5 m in five 1 m graduations. | FACTORY: The most implementable elevation in the article. Also the plate to measure from: in the 602x1036 Commons PNG the 5 m bar spans about 195 px, i.e. ~39 px/m (cross-checked against the two human figures at ~1.65 m). From that the column A shaft reads ~1.0 m diameter and ground-to-abacus ~3.7 m, vault springing ~14.5 m - measured from the plate, +/-10%, NOT from the text. | VERIFICATION: re-opened. Detail U, the stone wedge a between abacus and voussoirs, flyers L and S, column V on the triforium wall, pier X corbelled over Y, the 5 m bar and the two human figures are all present as described. But the anticipated-settlement INTENT read into them is Viollet's conjecture and he concedes 'trop subtil' - model the geometry, discard the mechanism.

subject: Plan of the circular part of the choir of Notre-Dame de Paris (c.1165) with its double ambulatory; inset X = axonometric of a triangular vault cell
note: fig. 44 | DRAWING: Detail plan + axonometric inset | SEEN: Quarter/half plan. The hemicycle stands on SIX piers, the second ring has ELEVEN, the third FOURTEEN. Result: the archivoltes AB, BC and the doubleaux DE, EF, GH, HI, IP are all planted on nearly equal diameters, so all crowns reach one level. The ambulatory cells are TRIANGULAR in plan and each is covered on a SINGLE diagonal rib (BE, EC, FI, IE, EH, HD) - no crossed pair. Heavy buttresses K, L, M (drawn solid black, deep) alternate with lighter intermediate ones O, R, S. Inset X shows one triangular cell in axonometric with its web hatched. | FACTORY: Direct generator recipe for a double ambulatory: pier counts 6 : 11 : 14; alternate heavy/light buttresses; triangular cells with one diagonal each; the extrados carries a walkable floor falling outward. Main thrusts and loads go to KLM, secondary to ORS.

subject: Plan of the Saint-Leu-d'Esserent hemicycle: four monostyle columns, two stout and two slender

subject: The naive early springing: the first voussoirs of doubleau, two ogives and two formeret shafts simply arranged side by side on a broad abacus
note: fig. 46 | DRAWING: Perspective + detail B | SEEN: Axonometric of an abacus carrying, jigsaw-fashion, the separate moulded first voussoirs of several arches; their tails (queues) are visibly CLIPPED (ecornees) at A so they can sit beside each other and stay within their bed. At the right, the round base of the formeret shaft sits FLUSH with the abacus edge. Detail B (left) shows the setting-out: the front of the voussoirs/springers is always plumb with the upper square of the capital's corbeille; the square of the formeret shaft base is set flush with the abacus so the shaft face comes plumb with the corbeille square. | FACTORY: Two hard plumb-line rules for the springing, and the failure mode of the method: needs a wide seat and a very splayed capital; gives crushable springers with no cohesion; and diffuses the thrust so no single resultant can be located.

subject: Rib voussoir sections: on edge vs flat, and the evolution of the profile envelope
note: fig. 47 | DRAWING: Plan/section of voussoirs | SEEN: A = a voussoir set on edge (tall, narrow); B = the same cross-sectional area laid flat (wide, shallow) - A resists pressure far better. C = the mid-12th-century square envelope with mouldings inscribed, drawn as a full square. D/E-F-G = the later ogive section: narrower from E to F, keeping depth to G, its outer arris only a blunt edge or a plain roll (boudin) at G so the skew springing on the abacus no longer produces warped surfaces. H/L-I-M-K = the later doubleau section: great depth on edge from I to K, with enough flat width L to M to resist torsion, torsion being already restrained by the web. | FACTORY: Rib profile generator: bounding box parameterised as (width, depth) with depth dominant; width shrinks over time while depth is kept; outer arris blunted to ease skew springings. Section side lengths given in the text: 0.22 / 0.33 / 0.50 m.

subject: Why springers must have horizontal beds: an upper pier B standing over a vault C, with and without a tas-de-charge
note: fig. 46 bis | DRAWING: Construction diagram | FACTORY: A load-path constraint that DERIVES the tas-de-charge: the vertical footprint of everything standing above the springing must land on a horizontal bed.

subject: Setting out the arches of an oblong (barlong) bay: give the ogive and the doubleau the SAME radius
note: fig. 48 | DRAWING: Construction diagram | SEEN: Rectangle with A top-left, E top-right, C bottom-right, D at the centre. The rabatted diagonal AC is the full semicircle A-B-E (a plein cintre on the diagonal, radius AD = half the diagonal). For the doubleau on AE: carry AD along AE to get F, strike arc AG from F with radius FA = AD; carry AF from E to F' and strike EG from F'. The doubleau is therefore a two-centred (tiers-point) arch of the SAME radius as the diagonal, its crown G reaching close to the diagonal crown. | FACTORY: One-line generator rule: R_doubleau = R_ogive = 0.5 * bay diagonal, two centres offset from each springing by that same radius. Yields identical voussoir cuts for both ribs and near-level crowns without any trial and error.

subject: The full epure for the springer of a barlong bay: how the abacus plan is DERIVED from the springer bed, not chosen
note: fig. 48 bis | DRAWING: Epure (setting-out drawing), plan + rabatted elevations | SEEN: Right: A is set on the wall face; AD along the doubleau directrix equals the thickness of the doubleau voussoir and becomes the radius of the semicircle D'DD'; the doubleau section is drawn on plan; two parallels EF are drawn to the ogive directrices AC at a spacing equal to the ogive voussoir width, giving the ogives in plan; the points G where the ogive axes meet the semicircle D'DD' are taken as the ogive intrados. That contour IS the lower bed of the first springer. Only THEN is the abacus drawn - either square-return I-K-L or star-shaped I'-K'-L'. The leftover gaps H receive the formeret shafts. A single capital and a single column M can stand under it, the capital being a corbelled console throwing three baskets out of one astragal. Upper: the rabatted doubleau on NO and ogive on AC; P is where they cease to interpenetrate in plan; perpendiculars PP' and PP' give Q on the doubleau extrados, which is the level of the LAST springer bed; PQ is divided into courses (three shown: R, S, T and R', S', T'); at Q the first radial cut QV is drawn, above which voussoirs U are independent. Because the ogive is thinner than the doubleau, a small horizontal ledge remains behind its extrados at Q', useful for starting the web. Left: the bed contours a, b, c, e transferred to plan for the setter-out, with the inclined cuts d. | FACTORY: The single most valuable figure for a rib-springing generator. Ordered algorithm: (1) wall face point A; (2) doubleau voussoir thickness -> radius of the bundling circle; (3) ogive voussoir width -> parallel pair; (4) intersect -> springer bed outline; (5) abacus = offset of that outline (square or star variant); (6) leftover gaps -> formeret shafts; (7) find the plan point P where the ribs separate, project to Q on the extrados, divide PQ by bank height into N horizontal beds; (8) radial cuts above Q. Tightening the ogive axes toward A (sometimes meeting AT A) is the knob for a tighter bundle.

subject: The three superposed moulded springers of fig. 48 bis seen in perspective, plus the first free voussoirs
note: fig. 48 ter | DRAWING: Perspective / detail | SEEN: Three stacked springer blocks A, B, C on a foliate capital with an octagonal abacus. Each is one stone whose top bed carries the horizontally sliced, interpenetrating mouldings of all the ribs; the profiles are visibly MORE SEPARATED on each successive bed. C carries the cuts normal to the rib curves. Above, detached: D = a doubleau voussoir, D' = an ogive voussoir, henceforth identical to one another all the way to the keystone. | FACTORY: Confirms the assembly order and gives the visual law: the rib profiles emerge progressively out of a solid mass. A generator should compute, per bed height, the boolean union of the rib profiles swept to that level - the union is one blob at the bottom and N separate profiles at the top. | VERIFICATION: confirmed - three stacked one-piece springers A, B, C on a foliate capital, rib profiles progressively more separated on each higher bed, free voussoirs D (doubleau) and D' (ogive) detached above. Supports the 'abacus is DERIVED' claim, incl. Viollet's own parenthesis '(seulement alors)'.

subject: Vaulting an irregular hall: one row of piers, a wide bay A-B and a narrow one between pier B and wall CD, with all crowns stepping down imperceptibly
note: fig. 49 | DRAWING: Plan + rabatted arches | FACTORY: Explicit aesthetic constraint that becomes a generator constraint: crown heights across adjacent unequal bays must form a monotone, near-continuous sequence; permitted knobs are stilting the springing and pushing the diagonal slightly above semicircular.

subject: Four superposed springers on one column where the arches spring at different heights: springer courses carrying 1, 2, 0 and 5 rib cuts
note: fig. 49 bis | DRAWING: Perspective / detail | SEEN: Monocylindrical column, foliate capital, octagonal abacus, then FOUR springer courses. A = first springer, carrying the cut of ONE arch (doubleau EF). B = second, with the two cuts of the ogives EI. C = third, its upper bed COMPLETELY HORIZONTAL with no cuts at all. D = fourth, carrying the cuts of FIVE arches (two doubleaux PN, two ogives KL and the doubleau from pier A to pier B). Marked R on several courses: the RENFORTS - nibs of stone left in the springer courses behind the free voussoirs to receive the moellon web. | FACTORY: Proves the springer stack is a per-course table, not a uniform extrusion: course -> set of rib footprints (possibly empty). Plus the renfort: every springer course needs a web-bearing nib behind each freed rib. Both are cheap to encode.

subject: Vaulting an irregular quadrilateral with windows at very different heights - the fully parameterised case
note: fig. 49 ter | DRAWING: Axonometric + plan | SEEN: Irregular quadrilateral ABCD (A top-left, D right, B left, C bottom). The midpoints of the four sides are joined by GH and IK; their intersection F is the plan projection of the ogive crown. A vertical FE is raised and the crown level L chosen on it. The four ogives are then drawn as CIRCLE PORTIONS AL, BL, CL, DL, whose plan projections are AF, BF, CF, DF. The tall pointed formeret at the left is the 10 m window on face AB; a low semicircular formeret springing from the FLOOR ITSELF is drawn on the 8 m face CD. The dotted lines MN, OP, QR, ST are the ridge lines of the four web cells; the central keystone is assumed already placed. | FACTORY: The cleanest generator contract in the article: inputs = arbitrary convex quadrilateral + one crown height + per-face formeret crown heights; construction = midpoint lines to find the crown in plan, then one circular arc from each corner to the crown. Everything else (ridges, web) follows.

subject: Polygonal halls: pentagon, hexagon, octagon, canted-corner square, decagon - each divided into triangles by ribs from the re-entrant angles to the centre
note: fig. 50 | DRAWING: Plans (5 variants) | SEEN: Five plans stacked. In each, every re-entrant angle of the polygon is joined to the centre; those lines are the plan projections of the ogives, the polygon sides are the plan projections of the formerets. The 4th variant is a square with canted corners, which reads as an irregular octagon. | FACTORY: Trivial but exact: n-gon -> n triangular cells, one rib per vertex to the centre. Formeret crowns may sit above OR below the central crown as needed.

subject: Apse termination on a parallelogram: make the straight bay equal to one polygon side
note: fig. 51 | DRAWING: Plan | SEEN: The nave rectangle ends in a polygonal apse. A straight bay A-A is made EQUAL in length to one polygon side B-C, so the crown D is equidistant from B, C and E, and the triangles BCD and CED have BD = CD = ED. The arches A-D abut the radiating arches BD, CD, ED. All cells are triangles. | FACTORY: Sizing rule: last straight bay length = polygon side length. This is the condition that makes all radiating ribs equal and all crowns level, so it should be a hard constraint in an apse generator.

subject: The vicious exception: radiating ribs butting on the crown of a transverse arch, and the repair
note: fig. 51 bis | DRAWING: Plan | SEEN: Half of a ten-sided polygon. All the radiating ribs butt their heads at D', which sits on the crown of the doubleau GH and is NOT itself abutted, so they can warp GH. Drawn repair: two extra ogive branches ID' and RD' thrown from the corners of the last straight bay to abut D' powerfully. | FACTORY: A named failure mode with a named fix. A generator should detect 'radiating ribs converge on an unabutted point of another arch' and insert the two counter-branches.

subject: Plan of the porch of Notre-Dame de Dijon: arches of very unequal span with ALL crowns levelled, because a flat first-floor pavement sits on top
note: fig. 52 | DRAWING: Plan with rabatted arches | FACTORY: The complementary case to fig. 49 ter: fix all crowns to one plane and let the SPRINGING heights vary. Rule: springing_height = crown_level - rise(span), so wide arches spring lower.

subject: Perspective of pier M at the Dijon porch: one doubleau springing far below the others, its capital placed to suit
note: fig. 53 | DRAWING: Perspective / detail | FACTORY: Pier generator: capitals at multiple levels on one shaft, each level serving the arches whose spring height it matches.

subject: Horizontal section of a Romanesque pier at Peterborough with the abacus plan and the lower bed traces of every arch
note: fig. 54 | DRAWING: Plan | FACTORY: Anglo-Norman early-12c rule and a dating marker: segmental diagonals (less than a semicircle) to keep the diagonal crown DOWN, the exact inverse of the later French practice. Also: capitals divided into as many members as there are arches.

subject: Perspective of the Peterborough capital with the arch springings, and the geometral drawing of the ogive branch A, the common springer and the capital corbellings
note: fig. 54 bis / 54 ter | DRAWING: Perspective + geometral | FACTORY: Anglo-Norman variant of the springer: capital split into one member per arch, corbelled out from the pier section.

subject: THE web epure: how the courses of the moellon web are set out for a square bay crossed by an intermediate doubleau
note: fig. 55 | DRAWING: Epure (setting-out drawing), plan with rabatted extradoses | SEEN: Quarter plan, A at the corner, C the crown, D and E on the sides. Rabatted on the plan: the formeret extrados as the broken curve A-F-D including its raised (vertical) springing; the principal doubleau as E-G; the ogive as the exact quarter-circle A-I; the intersecting doubleau as D-H. A scale bar X-X' at the left is the width of a hand-manageable moellon. The formeret half A-F is stepped off with that unit, giving four rows and division points L, M, N; those are brought back onto the plan line AD as L', M', N'. The ogive half A-I is then divided into FOUR EQUAL PARTS - equal in number, not in size - giving O, P, Q, brought back to O', P', Q' on AC. Joining N'-O', M'-P', L'-Q', K-C by STRAIGHT lines gives the horizontal projections of the VERTICAL PLANES in which the intrados joints of the web courses must lie. The lower triangle ECJ is done the same way but with SIX divisions (U, V, Z and Y, Y', Y'), because the principal doubleau commands there. Rise conditions stated: with a semicircular ogive, the intersecting doubleau must have a rise CH equal to the radius CI; the principal doubleau a rise JG LESS than CI; the formeret, including its raised springing, a rise KF less than that of the principal doubleau. | FACTORY: The core web-coursing algorithm, fully specified: (1) the WALL ARCH commands - divide its rabatted extrados by the moellon width to get the course count n; (2) divide the diagonal's rabatted extrados into the SAME n parts (which are therefore larger); (3) join corresponding points; (4) each joint arris lies in a vertical plane. Also a rise ordering constraint: rise(intersecting doubleau) = R_ogive > rise(principal doubleau) > rise(formeret incl. stilting). | VERIFICATION: all joint lines (N'O', M'P', L'Q', K-C) confirmed running from the formeret plan line AD across to the diagonal AC, the last being the ridge K-C. The rise-ordering chain is verbatim. CORRECTION: Viollet divides the extrados of the HALF formeret - 'combien l'extrados du demi arc formeret AF, compris sa naissance verticale, contient de fois XX' : soit quatre fois' - so n=4 is courses PER HALF-CELL. The reader's headline said 'the formeret', which halves the course density. Note also the wikisource transcription reads 'conformement a l'epure tracee fig. 50' where it must mean fig. 55.

subject: The mason's master template arc drawn on a board: chord C'K' with rise ab
note: fig. 56 | DRAWING: Detail / template | SEEN: A nearly flat circular arc struck through three points C', b, K'. The chord C'K' is the length from the ogive crown to the formeret crown (CK or CJ of fig. 55); the perpendicular ab erected at its midpoint is the stated rise, 0.50 m. Nothing else on the plate. | FACTORY: Replaces the whole epure on site. The mason measures each course length with a string, lays that length off as a chord on this arc, reads the resulting rise, and uses it for that course. One number (0.50 m rise) drives every course of the cell. | VERIFICATION: the 0.50 m rise is an EXAMPLE value, not a constant - 'Le constructeur dit, PAR EXEMPLE : la ligne CK ... aura 0,50 c. de fleche'. The reader's figure note said 'one number drives every course of the cell' without the hedge; its dimensions entry had it right.

subject: The first third of a web cell rising 'like a wall' without any support
note: fig. 57 | DRAWING: Perspective / detail | SEEN: A springing seen from below-inside: the tas-de-charge with its horizontal beds, the ribs freeing themselves and running up as coursed voussoirs, and between them the first courses of the moellon web - laid with nearly horizontal beds, coursed like ordinary walling, standing unsupported. Stippling marks the mortar. Base moulding and plinth below. | FACTORY: Confirms the staged web build: cell = [zone 1, near-vertical, built as walling, no support] + [zone 2, built on the sliding cerce]. The boundary is at about one third of each side of the triangle. | VERIFICATION: confirmed - coursed near-horizontal-bedded rubble rising between the ribs. Text says 'au MOINS un tiers' (at least a third), a lower bound; the reader softened it to 'about one third'.

subject: The cerce: the extensible curved board that replaces centering
note: fig. 58 | DRAWING: Perspective / tool detail | SEEN: Two thin curved boards overlapping, each with a hollowed central GROOVE (rainure) concentric with the template arc of fig. 56; two keys/wedges C pass through the grooves and are tightened to lock the pair rigid, so the assembly can be LENGTHENED course by course by sliding one board against the other. Iron squares (equerres en fer) A and B are nailed at the outer ends, forming beaks that sit on the points previously marked on the ribs. Board thickness stated in the text as about 0.04 m. | FACTORY: A fully modellable medieval tool, and an important negative: no centering, no lagging, no falsework in the cell. Constraint recorded in the text: the two boards together must be LONGER than the ridge line of the cell, and one of them no longer than the most steeply inclined course that cannot be turned unsupported.

subject: Fig. 59: the cerce placed UNDER the joint line between two courses. Fig. 60: why the joint arris must lie in a vertical plane
note: fig. 59 / 60 | DRAWING: Details / geometric proof | SEEN: Fig. 59 (left): a run of moellon courses with the cerce and its key shown fixed beneath the SEPARATING joint line, not beneath the middle of a course. Fig. 60 (right): the cell triangle with A at the top of the vertical springing zone, B and B' at the foot, D at the far corner; near-vertical joint lines fan from the base line B-D up to the hypotenuse A-D; a dashed line C-D crosses them. Inset E = the resulting intrados face (douelle) of one course, a strip visibly wider in the middle than at the ends; inset G = the plan of a course, lens-shaped. | FACTORY: The generator consequence: because the intrados beds trace curves, the developed length of an intermediate section CD exceeds that of the base section DB which set the course count, so the surplus development must be spread over all the courses. Forcing the joint arris into a vertical plane does that automatically. Each web course is therefore a LENS: thicker at mid-length than at either end.

subject: Coursing of a hemispherical dome: concentric rings in horizontal projection
note: fig. 61 | DRAWING: Coupe + quarter plan | SEEN: A = the section, with voussoirs radiating from the centre; B = a quarter of the horizontal projection, the joints appearing as a family of CONCENTRIC CIRCLES with radial cross joints. | FACTORY: The alternative coursing topology (rings + radials) against which the Gothic web is defined. Needed because Viollet uses it as the ancestor of the Aquitaine and English webs.

subject: The first Aquitaine compromise: a web coursed as a DOME with diagonal ribs simply drawn across it
note: fig. 62 | DRAWING: Plan | SEEN: A square bay. The web joints are drawn as complete CONCENTRIC RINGS about the centre, exactly as in fig. 61B, taking no account whatever of the two diagonals, which are drawn straight across corner to corner and merely cross the rings. | FACTORY: The 'fake rib' state: ribs present, coursing ignores them. Text is explicit that such ribs 'ne portent rien, sont meme souvent engages dans les remplissages et maintenus par eux'.

subject: The second Aquitaine / Anglo-Norman state: courses sprung FROM the diagonals outward, crossing at the ridge, with a stone nerf added to hide the suture
note: fig. 63 | DRAWING: Plan | SEEN: A square bay with two diagonals and a central boss B. The web courses now take the EXTRADOS OF THE DIAGONALS as their bearing and run outward to the formerets and doubleaux, so that they INTERLEAVE / cross one another along the ridge lines from the formeret crown A to the diagonal crown B. A stone nerf is thrown from B down to F to receive the course ends and mask the sutures. Result: eight triangles instead of four, with a hollow re-entrant arris along AB. | FACTORY: The rival web-coursing rule, and the FUNCTIONAL ORIGIN of the ridge rib: it exists because the courses overlap and because the mason needed a wooden curve along AB to lean each course against. A generator that models this should emit the ridge rib automatically.

subject: The decisive comparison: half a bay coursed by Frenchmen, half by Anglo-Normans
note: fig. 64 | DRAWING: Plan | SEEN: One square bay, dotted centre line. LEFT half A: French - the web courses of each triangle run from the wall arch across to the diagonal, roughly perpendicular to the wall arch in plan and fanning slightly, meeting the diagonals and ARRIVING PARALLEL along the ridge. RIGHT half B: Anglo-Norman - the courses run off the diagonals outward, meeting the wall arches and CROSSING each other along the lines from the formeret crowns C, F, E to the diagonal crown D. The single central boss D serves both halves. | FACTORY: The clearest single image of the two coursing topologies. Should be the switch in a web generator: coursing_reference = 'wall_arch' (Ile-de-France, Beauvaisis, Champagne, 2nd half 12c) or 'diagonal' (Aquitaine, Anjou, Maine, England). | VERIFICATION: the two coursing topologies are genuinely as described (left half runs off the wall arches and butts parallel on the ridges; right half runs off the diagonals and interlaces along the ridges). POINT IDENTIFICATION CORRECTED: only C is a formeret crown - 'reunir la clef du formeret C a la clef des arcs ogives D par un nerf saillant masquant la suture formee par la rencontre des triangles de remplissage en moellon ECD, FCD'. E and F sit at the corners of the square where the diagonals land, not at wall-arch crowns; only C-D is the suture masked by the nerve.

subject: Three axonometrics: the bare Anglo-Norman rib skeleton, the Anglo-Norman web G, the French web H on the same skeleton
note: fig. 65 | DRAWING: Perspective (3 states) | SEEN: TOP: the bare ossature - two SEMICIRCULAR diagonals, four POINTED (tiers-point) formerets whose crowns sit BELOW the diagonal crown, plus ridge nerves running from each formeret crown to the centre. Viollet's reading: the Anglo-Norman vault is nothing but a hemispherical dome penetrated by four pointed arches. MIDDLE (G): the Anglo-Norman web on that skeleton - courses laid off the diagonals, producing four domical pendentive-like surfaces meeting along the ridges. BOTTOM (H): the French web on an IDENTICAL skeleton - courses laid off the formerets/doubleaux onto the diagonals, producing four distinctly CONCAVE triangular cells. | FACTORY: The best rendering reference in the article: identical rib geometry, two visibly different surfaces. Confirms that ribs alone do not determine the vault surface - the coursing rule does. | VERIFICATION: re-opened and cropped; panel G is a domical ring-coursed surface, panel H shows courses running from the formerets onto the diagonals with sharp concave ridges. Identical ossature, two different webs - the proof plate that rib_layout and web_coursing_rule are independent fields.

subject: Plan of the first bay of Mouliherne church near Saumur, where BOTH systems occur in one vault
note: fig. 66 | DRAWING: Plan | FACTORY: A hybrid test case: rib section = plain semicircular torus; two coursing rules in one bay; decorative ridge nerves that do nothing. Useful as a 'transitional west-of-France' preset.

subject: Section of the Mouliherne vault on line GS
note: fig. 67 | DRAWING: Coupe (section) | FACTORY: Section companion to fig. 66.

subject: Interior perspective of the Mouliherne vault
note: fig. 68 | DRAWING: Perspective | FACTORY: Rendering reference for the hybrid vault.

subject: Section of an Anglo-Norman vault: why raising the formeret crowns broke the ridge nerf, and the tierceron repair
note: fig. 69 | DRAWING: Coupe + plan | FACTORY: The stated STRUCTURAL reason for tiercerons: a near-flat ridge rib sags at midspan, so extra ribs are inserted to reach it. This is a mechanism a generator can honour - tierceron count as a function of ridge-rib flatness and span.

subject: High vault of the choir of Ely cathedral, mid-13th century: plan of the rib net with the web coursing hatched, and the section CD
note: fig. 70 | DRAWING: Plan + coupe | SEEN: Oblong bay E-F top and bottom. Upper half: the rib net - bosses G on the longitudinal ridge rib, tiercerons fanning from each springing, transverse ridge ribs. Lower half: the same net with the WEB COURSING drawn - the courses fan out from each corner springing in dense radiating sets, i.e. the surfaces are conoidal, not concave cells. Left: the section CD taken on C'-D', showing the formeret crowns C' and D' raised ABOVE the boss level G in order to take very tall windows. | FACTORY: Fan/conoid web preset. Note the inversion of the French rule: here the formeret crowns go ABOVE the diagonal crown, the opposite of both the early Anglo-Norman and the classic French arrangement.

subject: Perspective of a springing of the Ely choir vaults: the sheaf of curves and the concave conical surface
note: fig. 71 | DRAWING: Perspective | FACTORY: Rendering reference for the conoid springing.

subject: Plan of the Ely springing: the compact rib bundle at bed level A, the horizontal section C at level B, and the VERTICAL web panel forced by the high formeret springing
note: fig. 71 bis | DRAWING: Plan / detail | SEEN: A = the lower bed of the whole bundle of ribs on the abacus, drawn as a tight cluster of moulded profiles with circular rolls. C = the horizontal section at level B: from D to E it traces a portion of a polygon standing on the rib branches, but from D to F - F being the formeret - it RE-ENTERS ABRUPTLY, because the formeret springs far higher than the ogives, doubleaux and tiercerons. Consequently the moellon web G-F has to rise VERTICALLY in the plane through GF. Above, the two window/formeret shafts F stand well outside the bundle. | FACTORY: The geometric defect that drove the next step: a vertical, flat web panel beside conoidal surfaces. Viollet's jab: 'La presence de la surface FG verticale, a cote des surfaces courbes DE, n'etait pas logique pour des rationalistes.' A generator must handle this wedge whenever formeret springing > rib springing.

subject: The English resolution: all springings at one level, all crowns in one horizontal plane, ribs become portions of ellipses
note: fig. 72 | DRAWING: Axonometric with construction lines | SEEN: An oblong bay drawn in axonometric with a full grid of construction lines. All rib springings start at one level. The crowns A, B, C lie in a single horizontal plane. To achieve that with a common springing level the doubleaux and ogives had to become very DEPRESSED curves, drawn as portions of ellipses (several superposed curves are shown), while only the formerets keep a frank tiers-point. | FACTORY: Preset 'English 14c': springing_level = uniform, crown_level = uniform, diagonal and transverse ribs = depressed elliptical, wall arch = pointed. subject: The end of the line: a vault of interpenetrating inverted curvilinear cones (fan vault), intrados and extrados

subject: lock interior / mechanism
note: ANSWERS THE OPEN LOCK-MECHANISM QUESTION that Gardner could not: a drawn INTERIOR of a 12th-c serrure a bosse, cover removed. Read at 2400px upscale and keyed to Viollet's own text, which names every letter: the boite (case) is bounded by letters a b c d; the pele interieur p is joined to the pele exterieur P-prime by TWO STRONG RIVETS sliding in a coulisse cut through the pallatre; a turn of the key lowers the cramponnet c which blocks the bolt; a turn of the key FROM e TO f presses the ressort r and disengages the cramponnet, freeing the inner bolt. So e and f mark the START and END of the key's sweep, and the dashed circle in the figure is that swept arc. Viollet: 'Rien n'est plus simple que ce mecanisme, encore employe aujourd'hui.' CORRECTION TO MY FIRST READ: before fetching the text I took the concentric circle for a ward assembly and r for a tumbler; r is the SPRING and the circle is the key's rotation path. subject: lock, exterior + parts

Parts: pele A sliding between two riveted filets and held by two embrasses B; gache G receiving the bolt end; movable poignee P to pull the door; small bouton C to slide the bolt once the key has raised the cramponnet; box recessed into leaf V. TWO GENERATOR-RELEVANT DETAILS: filets are riveted on the pallatre both to reinforce it AND 'pour guider la clef, si l'on veut ouvrir la porte dans l'obscurite' (to guide the key in the dark); and the box is buried in a THICK door but its back shows on the outside of a THIN one - a thickness-dependent variant. Generally only one keyhole.

subject: The doublure/nerf stiffening principle - a lining bar welded to a hinge band ONLY at two c
content_type: schematic / generator diagram - elevation of a bar length plus one section
note: FIGURE NUMBER '8' IS LEGIBLE IN THE IMAGE (matches Viollet's fig. 8). NOT a portrait of a hinge - it is a pure stiffness diagram, which is why it is worth more to us than the named examples. Content: a length of flat band running the full width of the plate, closed at each end by a clasp lettered B (left) and A (right). Between the clasps the drawing shows the band and, laid along it, a second slimmer bar whose long edge is drawn as a free line with a visible gap - i.e. the two irons touch but are NOT joined along their length. Only under the two clasps do they become one body. Detail C below is the SECTION: an outer light rectangle (the clasp's wrap, drawn as thin outline) enclosing TWO separate hatched bodies - a tall full-depth rectangle (the main band) and, alongside it, a shorter bar with rounded ends (the doublure). A hairline of white separates them. So the lamination is FACE-TO-FACE on the flat of the band, the doublure is shallower than the band, and the clasp is a thin wrap band that goes right round both. MODELLING: Generator rule for any large hinge strap: main flat bar + a shorter, rounded-edged lining bar laid on its face, banded together at two (or n) points by a thin wrap collar, DELIBERATELY unattached between. Visually this gives a strap that reads as double-thickness with a fine parting line along its length, punctuated by plain collars. Do not model it as one thick bar and do not weld it continuously - the gap is the whole point (elasticity + stiffness + lightness). Section proportion from the drawing: doublure roughly 55-65 percent of the band's depth; clasp wrap thin, roughly one-fifth of the doublure's thickness.

subject: The BUNDLED BAND - a hinge band composed of several parallel rods welded only at clasps
content_type: schematic / generator diagram - elevation plus section
note: FIGURE NUMBER '9' IS LEGIBLE IN THE IMAGE (Viollet's fig. 9). This is the single most useful drawing for us. Elevation: band D running the width of the plate, terminated at each end by a clasp - I on the left, K on the right. Between the clasps the band is drawn as a run of roughly six long parallel arris lines, i.e. the flanks of the bundled rods, with slight irregularity along their length (hammered, not rolled). The LEFT clasp I is a plain wrap collar with a vertical row of about seven small half-round lobes cut or struck along it - the rod ends reading through the collar. The RIGHT clasp K is enriched: it carries a second, wider wrap outside it bearing a zigzag/lozenge chased ornament, and the band continues past it into the next member. Detail H below is the SECTION and is explicit: a thin flat plate down one side (the outer face of the band) and against it a stacked column of half-round lobes, bracketed in three groups labelled E, F and G - i.e. THREE rods, each of which sections as a doubled half-round (two lobes per rod), packed edge to edge behind one flat facing strip. Total six lobes for the three rods, matching the six arris lines in elevation. MODELLING: This is the profile authority for a great 13th-c hinge band. Extrude a section = one thin flat facing strip + a row of 3 rods each reading as a pair of half-round ridges (net effect: a REEDED / gadrooned strap of six ridges). Punctuate the extrusion at module boundaries with a plain wrap collar; every second or third collar is the enriched kind carrying an applied chased outer band. The reeding must run out UNDER the collars, never through them. Section stack order matters: flat plate to the outside (the face the viewer sees is flat-plus-reeds, and the reeds sit against the door side per the drawing's stacking).

subject: FIG. 2 - the C-form penture of the END OF THE 11th CENTURY: the seed form of the whole fam
content_type: elevation on the door leaf plus profile/section below
note: Figure numeral '2' is legible at top right. The board joints of the leaf are drawn as vertical rules across the whole plate, so the ironwork's relation to the frises is explicit. THE FORM: a single band bent into a near-closed C - almost a full circle, open toward the left - springing from a rectangular collet plate at B on the right and sweeping round to end, top and left, in two tight SCROLLED VOLUTES. The two arms are lettered A (upper) and A (lower); the extent of the boards they clamp is lettered C at the left. The band is drawn with fine parallel lines along its length (hammer flats / a slight central arris), it is broad and flat, and it is studded at intervals with small SQUARE-headed nails, drawn as little pyramidal studs standing on the band. At B there is a rectangular plate with what reads as a bolt or crampon head. BELOW, the profile: the band seen edge-on, very shallow and thin relative to its width, laid flat on the leaf, with the nail POINTS projecting through the far side as small wedges (to be clenched), and at the right end the rolled EYE drawn in section as a hatched ring set on a squared return - so the eye stands proud of the door face on a short square shoulder. MODELLING: The 11th-c hinge is a FLAT RIBBON, not a moulded bar: wide, thin, no reeding, no applied clasps, no bouquets. Its only ornament is the pair of terminal scrolls and the square nail heads. Build it as a planar C-curve (roughly 300 degrees of arc) offset from the eye, extruded on a wide-shallow rectangle, with the two ends spiralled tight. Nail spacing follows the board joints. Clench the nail points on the reverse - a visible feature on the inside of an authentic door. Compare against the later series: everything that arrives after this (branches, clasps, reeded bundles, swaged leaves) is an addition to this silhouette.

content_type: elevation of the hinge open/flat, with a small plan section and a dimensioned height
note: Figure numeral '42' is legible at top left. A DIMENSION IS LEGIBLE IN THE IMAGE: a vertical dashed dimension line marked '0, 27' - i.e. 0.27 m overall length of the hinge. Each leaf's outer profile is cusped and scalloped, and each terminates at the top in an animal / beast head with an eye and jaw. Both leaves are studded with large DOMED rivet heads, roughly a dozen per leaf, set in the solid webs between the piercings. Down the centre the two leaves each roll into knuckles: an upper knuckle group and a lower knuckle group, with a clear OPEN GAP between them where the PIN (the fiche) is exposed to view. The pin has a domed / bullet head standing above the top knuckle and a sharpened point below the bottom knuckle. Around the exposed middle length of the pin a ROUND-SECTION iron tail is wound in a long open SPIRAL, its two ends finishing in curled tips - free, purely visible, and the drawing shows it not attached to the leaves. subject: THE FORGED RIGHT-ANGLE JOINT for grilles: talon-in-fork closed by a keyed bolt, plus the s
content_type: perspective construction diagram with exploded fastener detail
note: FIGURE NUMBER '45' IS LEGIBLE. A tall square vertical bar crosses a horizontal bar in three-quarter perspective. At the crossing the vertical bar's top is split into a FOURCHETTE (fork) and the horizontal bar's end carries a TALON (a shouldered stub) that lands in the fork; the horizontal bar visibly SWELLS at the crossing to a wider collar-like boss rather than being notched away - the iron is gathered, not cut. Left of centre, exploded: the keyed bolt detail C - a bolt with a broad round head and a flat shank, and separately a tapered flat wedge (the CLAVETTE) that drops through a slot near the bolt's far end. Below it the same bolt shown assembled through the fork with a shaped washer under the head. Top right, detail B: a small orthographic square-hole-in-plate showing that the hole through which the square bar passes is a square hole in a swollen boss, with a moulded profile. Right of centre, A: the SAME joint dressed as ornament - the bolt head is now a domed boss and four long slender leaves sweep out from it over the joint, so the visible decoration is exactly the fastener. The bar's own arris is chamfered and the chamfers stop dead at the joint. MODELLING: Grille kit primitives, exact: (1) square-section bar; (2) fork end - split, spread and rounded; (3) talon - shouldered stub; (4) keyed bolt = round-headed pin + separate tapered wedge through a slot, wedge tip hammered over; (5) swollen eye = a local boss with a SQUARE hole for a square bar to pass. Rule from the drawing: at a crossing the bar gains section, never loses it, and the chamfer along its arris terminates at the joint. Ornament tier = replace the plain washer with a rosette and let 4 leaves radiate from the bolt head; nothing else changes.

subject: FIG. 14 - penture from the NORTH DOOR of the old cathedral of Carcassonne, c. 1320: the ea
content_type: elevation to scale with dimension line, plus section and eye profile
note: Figure numeral '14' is legible at top right. A DIMENSION IS LEGIBLE IN THE IMAGE: '0, 92' on the bottom dimension line = 0.92 m overall length of the strap. FORM: one long straight band that runs from a rolled eye at the right to a broad DIAMOND / spear-head terminal at the far left. Along its length the band swells three times into flat LOZENGE widenings (diamond-shaped pads), each pierced with domed-headed nails - two or three nails per lozenge, and single nails on the plain runs between. Near the left terminal, two very large flat SPIRALS spring symmetrically from the band, one above and one below, each coiling roughly two and a half turns inward to a tight centre; a small cusped shoulder marks where each springs from the band. Below the drawing, a separate enlarged spiral repeats one of them, next to a small triangular fragment. Detail A, right of centre: the SECTION of the band, drawn as a lens/leaf shape - thin at both edges and thickest at the middle, i.e. a central raised arris, not a flat rectangle. Bottom right: the eye in profile, showing the band running flat, then kicking up through a short S and rolling into a thick ring - an offset (detourne) collet. CRUCIALLY, THERE ARE NO CLASPS (embrasses) ANYWHERE ON THIS STRAP and no bundled bars - the band is single-thickness throughout. MODELLING: This is the dated hinge-form for the early 14th c and it is a completely different generator from the 13th-c type: no welded bouquets, no clasp collars, no reeded bundle. Recipe: single flat bar, lens-section (central arris), swelling to flat diamond pads at nail groups, terminating in a spear-head; two big flat volutes near the tip. All curves lie IN THE PLANE of the door. At 0.92 m long this is a real usable scale for a church door leaf. Absence of clasps is itself the dating signal - Viollet says the clasps that were habitual up to the middle of the 13th c are gon...

subject: WHY MEDIEVAL IRON IS TWISTED: two stiffness diagrams - equal-weight section reshaping, and
content_type: pure geometric diagram, two figures on one plate
note: TWO FIGURE NUMBERS ARE LEGIBLE: '47' (left group) and '48' (right group). Fig 47: A = a hatched SQUARE section, ruled into a 3x3 grid (the 0.03 m square bar of the text). B = two alternatives forged from the SAME weight of iron - an I-section (two flanges and a web) and a CRUCIFORM / plus-shaped section - each drawn on the same grid so the equal-area claim is visible. Fig 48: A = a plain square with both diagonals drawn, i.e. the bar bends across a face. B = the same square inscribed in a CIRCLE, with a fan of several chords drawn from the centre to the arc, showing the diagonal sweeping every point of the circumscribing circle as the bar is twisted. MODELLING: Justifies, from the source, the two most recognisable silhouettes in medieval ironwork. (a) Any load-bearing forged upright should read as I or cruciform in section rather than solid square - the flanges are structural, not decorative. (b) The twisted square bar is a STIFFENING device: model it as a square section swept along the axis with continuous rotation, which automatically produces the four CONCAVE hyperbolic faces Viollet notes; he also states the twisted bar is HEAVIER than the plain one for equal length but looks lighter because of those concave faces. Corollary for our kit: twist belongs on verticals that carry load (grille uprights, well-head posts), not scattered as ornament.

subject: FIG. 55 - the lower supports of the projecting SHOP GRILLE (cabaust) at Troyes, end of the
content_type: large-scale perspective of the corner assembly plus isolated component details

MAIN VIEW: the corner upright A and the wall-side upright B are flat bars, and their outward faces are CLAD IN ENGRAVED SHEET - the cladding is drawn covered in fine incised foliate scrollwork with small punched dots. THE TYPOLOGY, which is exactly what we needed to separate: (A) centre, the PAUMELLE - a SINGLE long plate; on its right edge, at mid-height, a projecting block carrying one knuckle. It has no partner leaf: it drops over a gond sealed in the stone. Its plate is pierced with hearts and cusped lobed voids, with round-headed fixings at the corners; a long plain reserve runs down the centre. A small profile below shows the plate with the rolled eye standing off it. (B) left, the true CHARNIERE - TWO mirror plates side by side, identically pierced, meeting on a common knuckle drawn with four or five interleaved barrels. This is the folding-leaf hinge (Viollet: 'Les charnieres reunis sont des vantaux brises'). (C) top right, the CHARNIERE-EQUERRE - the same pierced plate but with a horizontal arm crossing it at right angles and two lugs projecting on the far side, i.e. a hinge that turns a corner between rail and stile. (G) bottom right, the late-15th-century charniere-equerre: the plates are now cut into flamboyant foliage - a beast/dragon head terminal at the top of each, big curling leaf scrolls returning along the bottom rail - the knuckle is a long many-barrelled cylinder with a domed pin head, and the whole is clamped by TWO plain vertical BARRETTES laid over the plates, each studded with round rivet heads. Detail g shows one barrette alone: a narrow strip with a washer-and-rivet at each end. MODELLING: USE THIS TO STOP CONFLATING THE THREE. paumelle = one leaf + ...
