subject: FIG. 3 - THE TRIPLE-LIMB C-FORM PENTURE, beginning of the 12th century. FILENAME IS WRONG:
content_type: elevation on the door boards, dimensioned, with a section and a collet detail
note: Figure numeral '3' is legible at top right. TWO DIMENSIONS ARE LEGIBLE: '0,055' beside the section B (= 0.055 m, the width of a branch, matching the text 'En B, est la section d'une branche sur ab'), and '0,91' on the bottom dimension line (= 0.91 m overall). THE FORM, AND THIS IS THE GARDNER TEST CASE: from a single collet at the centre-right, THREE limbs spring. (1) A great near-closed RING sweeps right, up and over, round and back - drawn as two arcs (marked a on the outer, b on the inner) that together enclose almost a full circle across four board-widths. (2) and (3) The straight BAND runs left from the collet to a second cluster. At BOTH ends the limbs break into big paired VOLUTES: on the left, two mirrored S-scrolls with tight spiral eyes forming a lyre/heart; on the right, two more inside the ring. Two flared CUFF-COLLARS grip the straight band, one at each end of its plain run. NAILS: dozens of them, every one drawn as a SQUARE head sitting on a small square pad, set along the crown of every branch and all round the ring - the nailing is dense and follows the ironwork, and the door's board joints are ruled across the plate so the clamping across the boards is explicit. The section B is a LENS/leaf shape - thin edges, raised centre. DETAIL A, bottom: the collet shown in perspective passing RIGHT THROUGH the door timber and being welded/riveted on the far side. MODELLING: GARDNER'S TRIPLE STRAP IS HERE, VISIBLE: one straight centre limb plus two lateral curved limbs springing from a common collet - and Viollet's drawing shows the curved limbs closing into a ring rather than stopping as open crescents. Build recipe for a 12th-c church door: collet that passes THROUGH the leaf (not merely nailed on), three limbs, all branch ends resolved as tight volute eyes, lens-section bar 0.055 m wide, square nail heads on square pads at short intervals along every limb. ...

subject: FIG. 49 - THE GRILLE UPRIGHT (montant): a rebated post built of two core bars plus cheek p
content_type: elevation, face view, base plan/section, and exploded fastener details
note: Figure numeral '49' is legible at top right. DIMENSIONS ARE LEGIBLE ON THE PLATE: '0,49' on the vertical dimension line at the right, and '0,063' on the base detail A. RIGHT, elevation B: the post is drawn as TWO parallel core bars (the ame) with cheek plates (jouees) riveted on either side, so the post's outer faces form REBATES into which the grille panels slide. At two levels the cheeks swell into RENFORTS lettered e/K and l, each drawn as a leafy corbel-shaped projection with a DRIP (larmier) and, under it, a small shoulder - and in each shoulder a small rectangular SLOT is visible. From under the upper pair, at D, two ARCS-BOUTANTS spring and sweep down and outward in long ogee curves lettered g, splaying wide apart to reach the floor - and per the text each divides again lower down, so the two braces give FOUR anchorages. LEFT, face view F: the same post seen on its other axis, showing the row of slots up the middle and the overlapping DOUBLE KEYS pushed through them, and at the bottom the two brace feet h h passing through the floor line into their anchorages. TOP CENTRE, detail G: the double key itself, exploded - a flat plate pierced with two rectangular slots, with two curved leaf-shaped forked legs hanging from it. BELOW IT, H/m: the CLAVETTE - a small flat wedge, tapered along its length, with a rounded thickened head. BOTTOM, plan A: the section at floor level - the two core bars, the cheeks c and d, the brace feet splaying away, and the barlong (oblong) holes with the keys through them. MODELLING: This is the structural spine of any large grille or chapel screen. Post = 2 core bars + 2 cheek plates riveted on, giving a rebated section - so a grille's panels SLIDE IN and are never welded to the post, which is Viollet's thermal-expansion argument. Braces = long ogee flying buttresses, splitting to four ground anchors, resisting lean both in the grille's...

subject: FIG. 12 - THE EXPLODED SPINE of the low penture on the porte Sainte-Anne, Notre-Dame de Pa
content_type: exploded / disassembly diagram - the cleanest construction drawing in the article
note: Figure numeral '12' is legible at top left. The five modules are laid out in a single row with DELIBERATE GAPS between them so the joints are exposed, running right to left: A (the collet, its ends lettered a and b), B (the first member, c and d), C (the second member, e and g), D (the third member, k), and E (the terminal bouquet). EVERY MODULE IS DRAWN AS A BUNDLE OF PARALLEL BARS - long straight lines running the module's length, touching, unwelded between the ends. Reading the line counts: the collet A shows FOUR bars, the members B, C and D show THREE each, matching Viollet's text exactly. At EVERY module end the bars are gathered into a single heavily hatched PALETTE - a wide, flattened, slightly thinned scarf pad, drawn cross-hatched to show it is one solid mass where the bars have been welded together. Between the modules, pairs of long curved lines sweep away above and below: the secondary branches, springing precisely AT the module joints and not from the middle of a module's run. At the far left, E, the bundle resolves into a small spray of fine curling twigs. MODELLING: This is the authoritative build order and LOD scheme for a great 13th-c hinge, and it says three things a modeller would otherwise get wrong. (1) The strap is SEGMENTED - five modules, not one continuous bar - so seams belong at fixed intervals along it. (2) The bar count STEPS DOWN outward (4, then 3, 3, 3, thinner), so the strap tapers in DISCRETE JUMPS at the module joints rather than smoothly. (3) Branches spring AT the joints, because the joint is where the metal is already gathered - so branch attachment points and clasp positions are the SAME set of points. Author the strap as: [scarf pad][bundle run][scarf pad] x5, chain them, wrap every pad in a clasp, and hang the branches off the pads.

subject: FIG. 19 - penture drawn at Thann (Haut-Rhin), 15th century: hot-cut flat band with welded,
content_type: large-scale elevation of the central junction, dimensioned, with one profile detail
note: Figure numeral '19' is legible at top right. A DIMENSION IS LEGIBLE AND I CROPPED AND ENLARGED IT TO CONFIRM: '0,45' = 0.45 m. FORM: a wide flat band whose centre swells into a big cusped LOZENGE pierced right through with a QUATREFOIL - the hot-cutting technique of fig. 16 applied as an opening. From the lozenge, four heavy diagonal arms radiate; each arm is drawn as a flat tapering bar, and along its length small collar-BEADS with domed rivets mark the springing points of slender round-section stems. Those stems arch out and each ENDS IN A FLEURON, drawn as a squared cusped rosette - a lozenge with foliate cusps at the four corners and a large DOMED BOSS at the centre. There are more than a dozen such fleurons across the plate, and they are the dominant visual event. NOTABLY ABSENT: there are no clasps (embrasses) and no bundled bars anywhere - the band is single-thickness throughout. TOP RIGHT, a small PROFILE detail: the fleuron seen in section, showing that the domed boss stands proud on a short stalk above a low lobed cushion, i.e. the rosette is not flat but a two-stage relief. MODELLING: The 15th-c idiom: flat cut-and-pierced band, quatrefoil openings, and the visual weight moved entirely to the TERMINALS. The fleurons are the only parts still made by the old means - Viollet says they are welded to the stems, then swaged, then CHISELLED AFTER swaging, so their edges should read crisp and faceted while their domes read soft. Model each fleuron as a two-stage boss (lobed cushion + stalked dome) and each stem as a plain round rod. Nail every fleuron - they double as fixings. 0.45 m gives the scale. Contrast against fig. 3 (12th c) and fig. 12 (13th c) to see the whole arc: mass at the collet -> mass at the joints -> mass at the tips.

plate_title: Newel-less vis: half plan (A), section on CD (B), one step in perspective (G)
subject: stair, newel-less spiral
note: TEXT-KEYED. From the 14th c, where space was very tight, «on supprimait entièrement le noyau» - the newel is omitted entirely to free passage. The steps are simply superposed in a spiral and EACH CARRIES A BOUDIN AT ITS INNER END TO SERVE AS A HANDRAIL; where the newel would be there is «un vide». Figure gives half the plan at A, the section on line CD at B, and one step in perspective at G with dotted indication of unseen surfaces and the lower bed. A distinct stair TYPE for a generator, not a variant.

plate_title: Vis enclosed between columns, Mainz cathedral, mid-13th century
subject: stair, open-caged vis
note: TEXT-KEYED, and it settles what the figure does and does not state. Viollet: «nous donnons la moitié de son plan et UNE RÉVOLUTION ENTIÈRE. À partir du mur circulaire qui ne monte que jusqu'au niveau A, la construction consiste seulement en des MARCHES PORTANT NOYAU, et en des COLONNETTES, TOUTES D'ÉGALE HAUTEUR, soutenant chacune l'extrémité extérieure d'une marche.» So: newel integral with the steps; one colonnette per step, all of equal height, each carrying one step's outer end; the circular wall stops at level A. CRITICAL: the text gives NO COUNT of colonnettes or winders, so any per-revolution step count must be read off the figure and cannot be asserted from the text - which is why cycle 17's counts were refuted.

plate_title: Vis of the Reims tower pinnacles, perspective cutting diagram
subject: stair, tower vis in pinnacle
note: TEXT-KEYED, and it carries two hard rules. FABRICATION: «trois marches sont prises dans une seule assise» - THREE STEPS CUT FROM ONE COURSE, because the stone at Reims is enormous. LOAD PATH: stone chandelles B relieve the bearings A and sit over the step ends at C, but «PAR LE FAIT, C'EST LE NOYAU D QUI PORTE TOUTE LA CHARGE, et les pierres B ne sont qu'une suite d'étançons formant clôture à jour» - the NEWEL carries everything and the outer props are an open screen, not structure. Note this is the opposite emphasis from Mainz (fig 22), where each colonnette supports a step end: record them as two variants, not a contradiction.
